Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next

Chenghao Gao    Zhi Zhang    Dian Jin Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Data Science, National University of Singapore    Yihe Pan Affiliation: Department of Data Science, Fudan University*Equal contribution.†Corresponding author: doudouzhou@nus.edu.sg    Doudou Zhou Affiliation: Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of California, Los Angeles
Abstract

A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment’s dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO’s critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy’s probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent’s own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO’s 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.

1 Introduction

Agents trained with reinforcement learning on multi-step tasks often receive only sparse terminal rewards, which provide limited feedback for learning. Yet each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A needed object is found, an operation’s precondition is met, or a command is rejected, and the next observations record all these changes. When tasked with cleaning a plate and putting it in a cabinet, for example, an agent may find the plate and pick it up, but put it away without first cleaning it at the sink. The final reward marks the whole attempt as a failure. It does not say which steps helped, or which other action would have left the agent better placed to succeed.

World models learn environment dynamics by predicting how an agent’s actions change the environment. What a predicted change means for success depends on the task and on what the current policy can accomplish from the resulting state. In text environments, an action’s contribution to success is not necessarily reflected in how much the observation text changes. A transition that produces a very different textual observation may leave the chances of success unchanged: opening a cabinet, for example, may reveal a long list of objects unrelated to the goal. Conversely, a small change in the environment may establish a critical prerequisite or make the goal unreachable. Heating a mug, for instance, may produce only a brief confirmation, yet satisfy a necessary condition for a task that requires a hot mug. We therefore evaluate predicted transitions by their effect on eventual success.

Fortunately, PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) already learns such a valuation through its critic. The critic estimates the expected cumulative reward from a state under the current policy, and its evaluation evolves as the policy learns. When agents must learn from sparse terminal success rewards, the critic offers feedback before the task outcome is known. Its values estimate the probability of eventual success, and changes across a transition reveal how an action affects that probability. While PPO uses these estimates only through the advantages of executed actions, we apply the critic to the next states predicted by a world model for the policy’s candidate actions (Figure 2). These estimates, which we call transition values, let us compare the policy’s candidates through their predicted consequences. Diagnostics on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) support this idea: selecting among the policy’s candidates using these values achieves higher success than direct policy sampling (Section 2).

We therefore introduce WM-PPO, which incorporates this feedback through policy and value channels. At each state along the main training trajectory, the policy samples several candidate actions and executes the first as usual. The policy channel turns candidate comparisons into auxiliary advantages in PPO’s clipped objective, while the value channel uses the mean transition value as an additional one-step target for the critic at the current state. These critic updates also affect the advantages used in subsequent policy updates. Since value estimation in LLM reasoning can be biased and yield unreliable comparisons between candidate steps (Yuan et al., 2025; Kazemnejad et al., 2025), WM-PPO calibrates both channels against real outcomes. For each training task, it collects one main episode and three branches, each trying a different action at a randomly chosen step. A shared gate uses earlier branch outcomes to weight both channels according to the margin between transition values (Section 3). The design stays elegant: the world model is the only learned component added to PPO and reuses the real transitions collected during training. Real returns remain the critic’s main supervision. Training requires no teacher model or privileged information, and the policy acts alone at inference.

Prior work also draws on signals beyond terminal rewards to improve language agents (Table 3 in Section 6). Some methods add observation-prediction losses during RL (Shrivastava et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026), while others learn environment dynamics before downstream policy training (Zhang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026b). Distillation methods obtain finer feedback from teacher distributions or from models given hindsight observations or reference solutions (Agarwal et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). World models also provide imagined outcomes for action selection and refinement in WMA, ITP, and CoMAP, where they remain part of the deployed agent (Chae et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b). Internalizing the Future (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns from teacher-generated foresight traces. Its policy expresses confidence in an imagined plan before generating an action, and this confidence is calibrated against task outcomes to construct step-level advantages. ProAct’s MC-GRPO (Yu et al., 2026c) compares actions sampled at the same state using values estimated from simulator rollouts. WM-PPO instead evaluates candidates through their predicted consequences using a world model and PPO’s existing critic. Both networks learn from the agent’s own interactions, turning predicted state changes into feedback for policy and value learning.

We evaluate WM-PPO on the simpler ALFWorld and on the harder ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022), whose tasks often require establishing intermediate conditions before the agent commits to an answer. The comparisons test whether learning from predicted consequences improves success for a comparable amount of real interaction (Section 4). They cover PPO, its multi-turn refinements and group-based methods; structural controls that change one component at a time; and auxiliary supervision from observation prediction, agreement and teachers. The main table compares 17 methods and variants, and the interaction-efficiency analysis places WM-PPO among 23 other methods and settings on ALFWorld and 20 on ScienceWorld. We then analyze how the two channels affect learning, and how the trained policy advances a task (Section 5).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Learning from dynamics by valuing predicted consequences. We show that valuing world-model predictions with PPO’s critic turns information implicit in environment dynamics into feedback that supplements sparse terminal rewards. Diagnostics demonstrate that these transition values support both action selection and policy improvement.

  • •

    Calibrating value-based feedback with real outcomes. To account for noisy critic estimates, we use outcomes of real branches to calibrate a shared gate that weights both channels by how often comparisons with similar margins agreed with real outcomes earlier in training. The critic’s values thus reach both the policy and the critic itself as a stable signal grounded in real outcomes.

  • •

    WM-PPO: transition values for policy and critic learning. We introduce two complementary learning channels: comparisons among transition values provide auxiliary policy advantages, while their mean supplies an auxiliary critic target. Only the policy is needed at inference. On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, WM-PPO reaches PPO’s success levels with fewer real interaction steps and achieves higher success at comparable interaction budgets.

2 From Predicted Consequences to Learning Signals

We first relate state transitions to changes in the probability of success, then test whether predicted consequences can guide a policy update.

Setting.

A task is a natural-language goal in a text environment. At step tt the agent is in state sts_{t}, by which we mean the content of its prompt: the goal, its five most recent observations and actions, the current observation, and the actions or objects currently available. The policy πθ\pi_{\theta} samples a short response yty_{t}, from which one action ata_{t} is parsed. The environment returns the next observation ot+1o_{t+1}, and the next state st+1s_{t+1} adds ata_{t} and ot+1o_{t+1} to the history and refreshes the list of available actions or objects. The value of a state under the policy π\pi is the expected return that follows it,

Vπ​(st)=𝔼π​[∑k≥0γk​rt+k+1|st],V^{\pi}(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Bigl[\,\sum_{k\geq 0}\gamma^{k}\,r_{t+k+1}\Bigm|s_{t}\Bigr], (1)

where γ\gamma is the discount factor, rr denotes reward, and we treat sts_{t} as sufficient for predicting returns. In the environments we study, the only reward is the final reward R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\}, given at the last step: 1 if the task was completed within 40 steps and 0 otherwise. With γ=1\gamma=1, the value is then the probability of eventually succeeding,

Vπ​(st)=𝔼π​[R|st]=Prπ⁡(success|st),V^{\pi}(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\bigl[R\bigm|s_{t}\bigr]=\Pr\nolimits_{\pi}\bigl(\text{success}\bigm|s_{t}\bigr), (2)

and we write Vπ​(s)=RV^{\pi}(s)=R for a state that ends the episode. The superscript marks that these values belong to the current policy π\pi, so they can change as the policy learns. An intermediate transition from sts_{t} to st+1s_{t+1} receives no reward, yet it changes this probability by Vπ​(st+1)−Vπ​(st)V^{\pi}(s_{t+1})-V^{\pi}(s_{t}). The observation records what changed in the environment; the difference in state values measures how that change affects the current policy’s probability of success. The probability of success after an action is Qπ(st,a)=𝔼[Vπ(st+1)∣st,at=a]Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}[V^{\pi}(s_{t+1})\mid s_{t},a_{t}=a], and the action’s advantage is the expected change in state value caused by the action,

Aπ(st,a)=Qπ(st,a)−Vπ(st)=𝔼[Vπ(st+1)−Vπ(st)|st,at=a].A^{\pi}(s_{t},a)=Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a)-V^{\pi}(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[V^{\pi}(s_{t+1})-V^{\pi}(s_{t})\bigm|s_{t},a_{t}=a\bigr]. (3)

At a fixed state, the difference between two actions’ advantages is therefore the difference between their expected success probabilities. PPO estimates this advantage only for the executed action, through the critic’s values along the executed path (Appendix B.2). Estimating it for the alternatives requires their transitions, which a world model can predict.

The critic Vψ​(st)V_{\psi}(s_{t}) estimates Vπ​(st)V^{\pi}(s_{t}), and a world model pϕ​(ot+1∣xt,at)p_{\phi}(o_{t+1}\mid x_{t},a_{t}) predicts the next observation from its own view xtx_{t} of the history (Section 3.1). All models are LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025). The diagnostics use ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and the policy and critic of a PPO run continued from the common warm-up of Section 4.1 to iteration 24 (53.6% success on the 274 evaluation games); all evaluations are paired by game.

Equation (3) suggests three tests. The critic must order the successors of different actions by their probability of success; predicted successors must preserve these differences for actions that were not taken; and updates built on the comparisons must improve the policy when it acts alone. We test these conditions before introducing the online method.

2.1 Does the critic see the value of a state transition?

We first test whether the critic can compare actions at the same state by valuing their real successors. At every step, the policy samples four candidate actions. Each distinct candidate is executed for one step in a copy of the environment, and the critic values each resulting next state. The agent then executes the candidate with the highest-valued successor, which is expected to leave the greatest chance of success (Equation (3)). The policy is held fixed.

Selecting by the critic’s value of the real successor raises success from 56.9% (majority vote over the four candidates) to 70.4%, a gain of 13.5 points (SE 2.8, p<10−4p<10^{-4}; Figure 1a); executing a single sampled candidate gives 54.4%. Most of this gain comes from valuing intermediate successors: a control that selects a candidate only when it completes the task immediately, and otherwise uses majority vote, reaches 59.5%. The critic therefore carries information about intermediate transitions that the agent’s own choices do not use.

The reliability of this ranking depends on the gap between the critic’s values. Prior work reports noisy and initially biased value estimates that rank candidate next steps near chance (Kazemnejad et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025). At randomly chosen states, we executed each distinct candidate and estimated its success probability from three continuations. Of the 195 candidate pairs whose estimates differ, the critic orders 57% correctly, and the median gap between its two values is 0.008. Ranking accuracy increases from 53% in the lower half of the critic’s value gaps to 71% in the top quarter. Among the 12 pairs for which one candidate succeeded in all three continuations and the other in none, the critic ranked 11 correctly (Figure 1b). Large value gaps identify the comparisons the critic orders most reliably. The reliability gate uses real outcomes to determine how much weight each margin should receive (Section 3.5).

2.2 Do predicted state transitions preserve this value?

We next test whether learned dynamics make these values available for candidates that are not executed. A world model replaces the one-step execution: a separate LoRA adapter on the same base model, trained with a next-observation loss on transitions that the same policy generated on 1,000 training games. For this diagnostic only, its data also include one-step executions of candidates the policy did not choose (48k transitions, 44% of them for such candidates); the world model of WM-PPO is trained on executed transitions alone. At each step, the world model greedily predicts the next observation of every distinct candidate, and the critic values each predicted next state. The agent selects the candidate with the highest value and executes it in the environment; the other candidates are never executed.

Choosing by predicted consequences reaches 66.4%, 9.5 points above majority vote (SE 2.5, p<0.001p<0.001; Figure 1a) and close to the 70.4% obtained with the true consequences. With the untrained base model as the world model, selection reaches 61.7%; the trained model is 4.7 points higher. Two controls examine why selection with true consequences performs better. When the true next observation is combined with the action list from before the step, as in the world model’s successor, selection reaches 65.3%. When newly revealed objects are removed from the true observation, it reaches 59.1% (Appendix C). Both the refreshed action list and the newly revealed content contribute to the gain. The predictions are exact for 99.7% of the held-out observations that follow from what the agent has already seen, but for only 26% of those that reveal objects it has not seen; for the latter, they still give a prior over what will be found (Appendix C). In this diagnostic, predicted transitions preserve most of the selection gain obtained with real ones.

2.3 Can the policy learn from these values?

The final test asks whether the comparisons produced by the world model and critic can improve the policy itself. Starting from the same checkpoint, the policy played 500 new training games, executing the first of four samples at each step. At the 8,042 decision points with at least two distinct candidates, the candidate a^t\hat{a}_{t} preferred by the world model and the critic served as a label, and each of the four samples at(1),…,at(K)a_{t}^{(1)},\dots,a_{t}^{(K)} (K=4K=4) received the advantage

A~t,k=zt,k−z¯t,zt,k=𝟏[at(k)=a^t],z¯t=1K∑k′=1Kzt,k′.\tilde{A}_{t,k}=z_{t,k}-\bar{z}_{t},\qquad z_{t,k}=\mathbf{1}\bigl[a_{t}^{(k)}=\hat{a}_{t}\bigr],\qquad\bar{z}_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}z_{t,k^{\prime}}. (4)

These advantages sum to zero across the samples at each decision point. One epoch of PPO-clip on these samples used no task reward. The updated policy was then evaluated alone, at temperature 1, twice on the 274 games.

The update raises policy-only success from 57.1% to 65.3% (+8.2 points, SE 2.0, p=0.0003p=0.0003; Figure 1c). Using majority-vote labels on the same data for the same number of updates gives 56.9%, no change from 57.1%, although the two sets of labels agree at 44% of the decision points. With the data and update count held fixed, the consequence-based labels supply the information that improves the policy. The gain persists when the updated policy acts alone, without the world model or the critic.

From diagnostics to an online method.

Starting from a fixed policy, the diagnostics show that the critic can compare actions by valuing their successors, that the world model extends this evaluation to unexecuted candidates, and that the policy learns from the resulting comparisons. Reliability depends on the value margin, so the comparisons must be calibrated against real outcomes. As the policy improves, it visits new states and proposes new actions, requiring the world model, critic and reliability estimates to be updated. WM-PPO brings these steps into online training and uses the transition values for both candidate comparisons and critic targets.

3 WM-PPO

WM-PPO adds one learned component to PPO: a world model pϕp_{\phi} trained on real state transitions to predict the next observation after an action. The policy πθ\pi_{\theta} keeps PPO’s clipped objective, and the critic VψV_{\psi} learns primarily from real returns. At each training state, the world model predicts the consequences of the policy’s candidate actions, and the critic values the predicted successors. These transition values enter learning through two channels. Comparisons among the candidates supply auxiliary advantages for the policy (the policy channel), and the mean transition value supplies a one-step target for the critic (the value channel). Small rollout trees provide real branch outcomes, and a gate uses earlier branches to weight both channels by the reliability of their value margins. Section 3.1 defines the evaluation, Sections 3.2 and 3.3 the two channels, Section 3.4 the training loop, and Section 3.5 the gate. Figure 2 gives an overview, and Algorithm 1 summarizes one iteration (Algorithm 2 in Appendix B.1 gives the full procedure).

3.1 Evaluating predicted state transitions

The state sts_{t} is what the agent sees in its prompt at step tt: the task, the step counter, the five most recent observations and actions, the current observation, and the admissible actions (ALFWorld) or the objects that can be referred to (ScienceWorld). It is not the simulator’s internal state, which no model sees. At a state sts_{t} reached during training, the policy samples KK responses yt(1),…,yt(K)y_{t}^{(1)},\dots,y_{t}^{(K)} at temperature 1, and the actions at(1),…,at(K)a_{t}^{(1)},\dots,a_{t}^{(K)} are parsed from them. The first action is executed, at=at(1)a_{t}=a_{t}^{(1)} with response yt=yt(1)y_{t}=y_{t}^{(1)}, so collecting the candidates leaves the behavior policy unchanged. The success probability after an action and the value of a state (Equation (2)) are related by

Qπ(st,a)=𝔼[Vπ(st+1)|st,at=a],Vπ(st)=𝔼a∼π(⋅∣st)[Qπ(st,a)],Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[V^{\pi}(s_{t+1})\bigm|s_{t},a_{t}=a\bigr],\qquad V^{\pi}(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{t})}\bigl[Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a)\bigr], (5)

where Vπ​(st+1)=RV^{\pi}(s_{t+1})=R if the step ends the episode. When at least two candidates differ, the world model predicts the next observation of each distinct candidate aa (Figure 2a), a successor state is assembled from the prediction, and the candidate is valued:

o^t+1(a)=greedypϕ(⋅∣xt,a),s^t+1(a)=C(st,a,o^t+1(a)),q^t​(a)={1if o^t+1​(a) reports that the task is completed0if o^t+1​(a) reports that the episode has ended without completionVψ​(s^t+1​(a))otherwise.\begin{gathered}\hat{o}_{t+1}(a)=\operatorname{greedy}\,p_{\phi}\bigl(\cdot\mid x_{t},a\bigr),\qquad\hat{s}_{t+1}(a)=C\bigl(s_{t},a,\hat{o}_{t+1}(a)\bigr),\\ \hat{q}_{t}(a)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\hat{o}_{t+1}(a)$ reports that the task is completed}\\ 0&\text{if $\hat{o}_{t+1}(a)$ reports that the episode has ended without completion}\\ V_{\psi}\bigl(\hat{s}_{t+1}(a)\bigr)&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\end{gathered} (6)

We call q^t​(a)\hat{q}_{t}(a) the transition value of aa: the estimated value of the successor predicted for that action. It approximates Qπ​(st,a)Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a) in Equation (5) using one predicted next observation. The change in state value across a transition also subtracts the current-state value. A predicted ending gives its outcome directly, without a value estimate; otherwise the critic values the predicted successor. Only ScienceWorld’s observations report the end of an episode, so in ALFWorld every transition value is a critic value.

The world model’s context xtx_{t} uses the same interaction history as sts_{t} with a different window: all previous observations and actions in ALFWorld, and the last eight actions without their observations in ScienceWorld. It also contains the task, the current observation and the admissible actions or objects. The prediction is one greedy decode of the next observation as the environment would print it. In ScienceWorld, this observation includes the room, the inventory, the game’s progress score and, when the simulator ends the episode, a completion or failure marker.

The deterministic prompt constructor CC appends the candidate and the predicted observation to the history, advances the step counter, and updates the window of recent steps. The list of admissible actions or objects is carried over from before the step; only the observation is predicted. A real next state instead contains a refreshed list. Valuing an action through the state it leads to is the afterstate evaluation used when the effect of a move is known, as in backgammon (Tesauro, 1995; Sutton & Barto, 2018); here the effect is predicted. Appendix G gives complete model inputs and outputs for one evaluated state (Figure 19).

Equation (5) underlies both channels of WM-PPO. By the first relation, differences between the candidates’ transition values estimate differences between their action values; the policy channel uses them to rank the candidates (Section 3.2). By the second, the mean transition value estimates the value of the state and serves as a critic target (Section 3.3). For two candidates at the same state, the difference between their advantages in Equation (3) equals the difference between the success probabilities after them,

Aπ​(st,at(k))−Aπ​(st,at(k′))=Qπ​(st,at(k))−Qπ​(st,at(k′))≈q^t​(at(k))−q^t​(at(k′)).A^{\pi}\bigl(s_{t},a_{t}^{(k)}\bigr)-A^{\pi}\bigl(s_{t},a_{t}^{(k^{\prime})}\bigr)=Q^{\pi}\bigl(s_{t},a_{t}^{(k)}\bigr)-Q^{\pi}\bigl(s_{t},a_{t}^{(k^{\prime})}\bigr)\approx\hat{q}_{t}\bigl(a_{t}^{(k)}\bigr)-\hat{q}_{t}\bigl(a_{t}^{(k^{\prime})}\bigr). (7)

The common term Vπ​(st)V^{\pi}(s_{t}) cancels, so the comparison does not depend on how well the critic values the current state. The approximation uses a single predicted observation in place of an expectation, a learned critic in place of VπV^{\pi}, and truncated prompts with the previous action list in place of full states. Section 3.5 checks the resulting comparisons against real outcomes. A preferred candidate need not increase the value in absolute terms; it only has to do better than the other candidates the policy proposed. The critic outputs an unconstrained scalar and is trained toward the probability of success; its estimates may fall outside [0,1][0,1].

3.2 From value comparisons to policy updates

Among the distinct sampled actions, the preferred candidate is a^t=arg⁡maxa​q^t​(a)\hat{a}_{t}=\arg\max_{a}\hat{q}_{t}(a), whose predicted successor has the highest estimated probability of success. The margin mt=q^t​(a^t)−maxa≠a^t⁡q^t​(a)m_{t}=\hat{q}_{t}(\hat{a}_{t})-\max_{a\neq\hat{a}_{t}}\hat{q}_{t}(a) measures how clearly it is preferred; a tie at the highest transition value (mt=0m_{t}=0) gives no preference. Each of the KK sampled responses receives an auxiliary advantage, which is the advantage A~t,k\tilde{A}_{t,k} of the diagnostic in Section 2.3 (Equation (4)) scaled by a reliability weight:

At,kaux=νwℓ⁡(mt)(zt,k−z¯t),zt,k=𝟏[at(k)=a^t],z¯t=1K∑k′=1Kzt,k′,A^{\mathrm{aux}}_{t,k}=\nu\,w_{\ell(m_{t})}\bigl(z_{t,k}-\bar{z}_{t}\bigr),\qquad z_{t,k}=\mathbf{1}\bigl[a_{t}^{(k)}=\hat{a}_{t}\bigr],\qquad\bar{z}_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}z_{t,k^{\prime}}, (8)

where ℓ⁡(mt)\ell(m_{t}) is the margin bin into which mtm_{t} falls, wℓ∈[0,1]w_{\ell}\in[0,1] is that bin’s reliability weight (Section 3.5), and ν\nu sets the strength of the auxiliary term relative to the PPO term.

Duplicate actions share one prediction, but advantages are assigned to all KK responses, duplicates included. The samples of the preferred candidate receive the positive advantage ν​wℓ⁡(mt)​(1−z¯t)\nu\,w_{\ell(m_{t})}(1-\bar{z}_{t}), and the other samples the negative advantage −ν​wℓ⁡(mt)​z¯t-\nu\,w_{\ell(m_{t})}\bar{z}_{t}; the weight scales both. Because the advantages sum to zero within the state (Figure 2c), the update moves probability from the other sampled responses toward those of the preferred candidate. At the start of an update, when every probability ratio is 1 and no clipping applies, the auxiliary advantages give the gradient direction

∑k=1K(zt,k−z¯t)∇θlogπθ(yt(k)∣st)=1K∑k:zt,k=1∑k′:zt,k′=0∇θlogπθ​(yt(k)∣st)πθ​(yt(k′)∣st),\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(z_{t,k}-\bar{z}_{t}\bigr)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{t}^{(k)}\mid s_{t}\bigr)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k:\,z_{t,k}=1}\ \sum_{k^{\prime}:\,z_{t,k^{\prime}}=0}\nabla_{\theta}\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{t}^{(k)}\mid s_{t}\bigr)}{\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{t}^{(k^{\prime})}\mid s_{t}\bigr)}, (9)

scaled by ν​wℓ⁡(mt)\nu\,w_{\ell(m_{t})} and the token normalization of Equation (10). Each term raises the log-probability of a response with the preferred action relative to another sampled response at the same state, a pairwise preference. The size of the margin enters only through the bin’s weight: the policy learns which candidate is preferred, not by how much. Equation (8) is the group-relative advantage of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) without division by the standard deviation, computed among the samples of one state with a label of 1 for the preferred candidate. Free-text actions cannot be enumerated, and PPO learns a state-value critic. We therefore evaluate the KK samples through their predicted successors and retain only which candidate is preferred (related methods in Section 6).

The policy is trained on two kinds of examples, each a (state, response, advantage) triple. Ordinary PPO examples (st,yt,A^t)(s_{t},y_{t},\hat{A}_{t}) come from the executed steps. We compute their advantages by tree GAE on real returns (Section 3.4), which gives raw estimates AtGAEA^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t}, and whiten these over the executed steps to obtain A^t\hat{A}_{t}. Auxiliary examples (st,yt(k),At,kaux)(s_{t},y_{t}^{(k)},A^{\mathrm{aux}}_{t,k}) come from the evaluated candidates; their advantages are given by Equation (8) and are not whitened. A minibatch ℬ\mathcal{B} containing both kinds of example enters one clipped objective:

ℒPPO(θ)=−1N∑(s,y,A)∈ℬ∑i=1|y|min(ρiA,clip(ρi,1−ϵlo,1+ϵhi)A),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{(s,y,A)\in\mathcal{B}}\ \sum_{i=1}^{|y|}\min\!\Bigl(\rho_{i}A,\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}})A\Bigr), (10)

where ρi=πθ​(yi∣s,y<i)/πold​(yi∣s,y<i)\rho_{i}=\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid s,y_{<i})/\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i}\mid s,y_{<i}) is the probability ratio of the ii-th response token, πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} is the sampling policy, N=∑(s,y,A)∈ℬ|y|N=\sum_{(s,y,A)\in\mathcal{B}}|y| is the number of response tokens in the minibatch, and ϵlo,ϵhi\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}} are the clipping bounds (Yu et al., 2025). For a positive advantage, the clipping removes the incentive to raise a token’s probability ratio above 1+ϵhi1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}; for a negative advantage, it removes the incentive to lower the ratio below 1−ϵlo1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}. An executed response can appear both as an ordinary example and as an auxiliary example. States whose bin has weight 0, and tied states, contribute no auxiliary examples. We use K=4K=4, ν=1\nu=1 and (ϵlo,ϵhi)=(0.2,0.28)(\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}})=(0.2,0.28). The world model’s text predictions and the critic’s values are fixed before the update. Gradients reach the policy through its log-probabilities of the sampled responses.

3.3 From predicted transitions to value targets

The value channel uses predicted consequences to estimate how likely the current state is to lead to success. By the second part of Equation (5), the value of a state is the policy’s average action value. The KK samples are draws from πθ(⋅∣st)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) and q^t​(a)\hat{q}_{t}(a) estimates Qπ​(st,a)Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a), so their mean

q¯t=1K​∑k=1Kq^t​(at(k))\bar{q}_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{q}_{t}\bigl(a_{t}^{(k)}\bigr) (11)

is a one-step model-based estimate of Vπ​(st)V^{\pi}(s_{t}): the critic’s own values one step ahead, averaged over the actions the policy proposes, with predicted endings valued at 1 or 0. This estimate supplies an auxiliary critic target, weighted by reliability,

ℒcons​(ψ)=β​∑st∈𝒟wℓ⁡(mt)​(Vψ​(st)−sg⁡[q¯t])2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\psi)=\beta\sum_{s_{t}\in\mathcal{D}}w_{\ell(m_{t})}\bigl(V_{\psi}(s_{t})-\operatorname{sg}[\bar{q}_{t}]\bigr)^{2}, (12)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the set of evaluated chain states with mt>0m_{t}>0, sg\operatorname{sg} stops the gradient, and wℓ⁡(mt)w_{\ell(m_{t})} is the gate weight that also scales the state’s auxiliary advantages; we use β=0.5\beta=0.5. Like the transition values, the target is computed with the critic before the update. The term is added to the critic’s regression on returns (Equation (13)), which remains the critic’s main supervision. The two targets average over different things. The return target G⁡(st)G(s_{t}) averages the final rewards of the few episodes that pass through sts_{t}, all of which follow the executed actions, whereas q¯t\bar{q}_{t} averages over the KK actions the policy proposed, each valued at its predicted successor. Where the world model predicts an ending, the target includes the predicted outcome directly, also for candidates that were not executed.

Both channels reuse the same predictions, critic and gate. Write the transition value of each sample as q^t​(at(k))=q¯t+(q^t​(at(k))−q¯t)\hat{q}_{t}(a_{t}^{(k)})=\bar{q}_{t}+\bigl(\hat{q}_{t}(a_{t}^{(k)})-\bar{q}_{t}\bigr). The value channel trains the critic on the mean, an estimate of how good the state is under the current policy. The policy channel uses the ordering of the deviations to form the gated preferences in Equation (8); both these deviations and the auxiliary advantages sum to zero over the KK samples. The value channel also affects the policy through the critic. PPO’s advantages are built from critic-value differences along the executed path (Section 3.4), so a critic that values states more accurately can give PPO’s own update better advantages. This effect starts from the next iteration, because each iteration’s advantages are computed before its critic update. We call the method with both channels WM-PPO, and the variant without the term of Equation (12) WM-PPO (policy channel only).

3.4 Learning through real interaction

Each iteration uses one batch of branched real rollouts. Actions and returns train the policy and critic, observed transitions train the world model, and paired outcomes calibrate the gate (Figure 2; Table 4 in Appendix B).

Episodes and branches.

Each iteration draws 64 training tasks. For each task, the policy plays one main episode, the chain, in which every step also records the KK candidates. The policy then plays three branches from the chain. For each branch, we draw a step of the chain uniformly at random. Because the environments are deterministic, replaying the chain’s actions up to that step restores its state. We resample the policy’s first response at this state up to eight times, stopping when its action differs from the chain’s, and then continue the branch to the end. If all eight samples repeat the chain’s action, the branch continues with that action but yields no comparison. The policy proposed a different action within eight samples in 62–67% of the branches on ScienceWorld and in 40–61% on ALFWorld. Each iteration therefore plays 256 episodes. Branching from intermediate states to obtain real outcomes for different actions is common in tree-based RL for language models (Ji et al., 2026; Hou et al., 2025). Here the branches add real interaction to the PPO update and test the candidate comparisons against real outcomes (Figure 2b; Section 3.5). The resampled action enters PPO as an ordinary sample with its unconditioned log-probabilities (Section 7).

Critic.

The episodes of a task form a tree whose nodes are states and whose edges are executed steps; an edge shared by several episodes, such as the chain’s prefix before a branch point, appears once. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the set of nodes in the iteration’s trees and G⁡(s)G(s) the mean final reward of the episodes that pass through node ss. The critic minimizes

ℒV​(ψ)=∑s∈𝒮(Vψ​(s)−G⁡(s))2+ℒcons​(ψ),\mathcal{L}_{V}(\psi)=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\bigl(V_{\psi}(s)-G(s)\bigr)^{2}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cons}}(\psi), (13)

that is, a regression on returns plus the value channel of Equation (12), which the policy-channel-only variant omits (Appendix B.2 gives implementation details of the regression). PPO’s advantages are computed by GAE (Schulman et al., 2016) on the tree, with γ=1\gamma=1 and parameter λ\lambda. An edge ee from sts_{t} receives

AGAE​(e)={R−Vψ​(st)if e ends the episode,Vψ​(st+1)−Vψ​(st)+λ​A¯GAE​(st+1)if e leads to st+1,A^{\mathrm{GAE}}(e)=\begin{cases}R-V_{\psi}(s_{t})&\text{if $e$ ends the episode,}\\[2.0pt] V_{\psi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\psi}(s_{t})+\lambda\,\overline{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}}(s_{t+1})&\text{if $e$ leads to $s_{t+1}$,}\end{cases} (14)

where A¯GAE​(s)=|ℰ⁡(s)|−1​∑e′∈ℰ⁡(s)AGAE​(e′)\overline{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}}(s)=|\mathcal{E}(s)|^{-1}\sum_{e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}(s)}A^{\mathrm{GAE}}(e^{\prime}) is the mean raw advantage of the edges ℰ⁡(s)\mathcal{E}(s) leaving ss. On a path without branches, this is the usual GAE recursion. Its term Vψ​(st+1)−Vψ​(st)V_{\psi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\psi}(s_{t}) is the critic’s estimate of the change in state value across the executed transition (Equation (3)). The executed step tt of an episode receives the raw advantage AtGAEA^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t} of its edge. An episode cut at the step limit ends with R=0R=0, without bootstrapping. We use λ=0.95\lambda=0.95.

World model.

The world model is trained on the state transitions that the policy executes in training tasks, with the cross-entropy of the next observation given the world model’s context and the action,

ℒWM(ϕ)=−1No∑(xt,at,ot+1)∈ℬWM∑i=1|ot+1|logpϕ(ot+1,i∣xt,at,ot+1,<i),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WM}}(\phi)=-\frac{1}{N_{o}}\sum_{(x_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1})\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{WM}}}\ \sum_{i=1}^{|o_{t+1}|}\log p_{\phi}\bigl(o_{t+1,i}\mid x_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1,<i}\bigr), (15)

where ℬWM\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{WM}} is a minibatch of executed transitions, ot+1,io_{t+1,i} the ii-th token of the observation the environment printed, and NoN_{o} the number of observation tokens in the minibatch. The initial world model is trained at the end of iteration 12 on the executed transitions of the common PPO warm-up (Section 4.1). Afterward, each iteration’s executed transitions from chains and branches update it for one epoch, in parallel with the policy update; replayed prefix steps are not added again. Every recorded observation supervises what an action changed, whether or not the episode succeeded. This training reuses the interaction collected for RL and follows the states and actions of the current policy.

3.5 Reliability calibration and the complete training loop

Section 2 shows that value margins carry information about comparison reliability. Both the policy-dependent values VπV^{\pi} and the models estimating them change during training, so the gate recalibrates the margins in every iteration using recent real outcomes. The first step of every branch that obtained a different action provides a test (Figure 3a). At the same state sts_{t}, the chain took action atcha_{t}^{\mathrm{ch}} and the branch took atbr≠atcha_{t}^{\mathrm{br}}\neq a_{t}^{\mathrm{ch}}, and both continuations were played to the end, with returns GchG^{\mathrm{ch}} and GbrG^{\mathrm{br}}. Before the iteration’s update, the world model and the critic value both actions as in Equation (6). We write Δ​q^=q^t​(atch)−q^t​(atbr)\Delta\hat{q}=\hat{q}_{t}(a_{t}^{\mathrm{ch}})-\hat{q}_{t}(a_{t}^{\mathrm{br}}) and Δ​G=Gch−Gbr\Delta G=G^{\mathrm{ch}}-G^{\mathrm{br}}. The pair’s margin |Δ​q^||\Delta\hat{q}| assigns it to one of three bins ℓ=1,2,3\ell=1,2,3, ordered from the smallest to the largest margins, whose boundaries are the 0.5 and 0.8 quantiles of that iteration’s nonzero candidate margins mtm_{t} (Figure 3b).

For bin ℓ\ell, the realized gain of following the preference is

gℓ=1nℓ​∑pairs in bin ​ℓΔ​G​sign⁡(Δ​q^),g_{\ell}=\frac{1}{n_{\ell}}\sum_{\text{pairs in bin }\ell}\Delta G\,\operatorname{sign}(\Delta\hat{q}), (16)

computed over the nℓn_{\ell} pairs that the previous MM iterations stored in the bin, each with the value difference and bin recorded in its own iteration. The gain is positive when the preferred actions led to better real outcomes. Because final rewards lie in {0,1}\{0,1\}, Δ​G∈{−1,0,1}\Delta G\in\{-1,0,1\}, and a pair contributes only when its two outcomes differ. A bin thus earns weight when its comparisons often decide the task and its preferences are then usually right (Section 5.1).

The gate shrinks and rescales this gain to a weight capped at 1 (Figure 3c),

wℓ={clip⁡(nℓnℓ+n0⋅gℓgref, 0, 1),nℓ≥nmin,0,nℓ<nmin.w_{\ell}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\dfrac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}+n_{0}}\cdot\dfrac{g_{\ell}}{g_{\mathrm{ref}}},\,0,\,1\right),&n_{\ell}\geq n_{\min},\\[6.0pt] 0,&n_{\ell}<n_{\min}.\end{cases} (17)

Here n0n_{0} sets how strongly a bin with few pairs is shrunk toward zero, grefg_{\mathrm{ref}} is the shrunken gain at which a bin receives full weight, and nminn_{\min} is the number of pairs below which a bin stays closed. A bin whose comparisons do not pay off in real outcomes thus contributes nothing. We use M=4M=4, n0=40n_{0}=40, gref=0.05g_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.05 and nmin=20n_{\min}=20; these values were set once from the first branch pairs of a preliminary ALFWorld run and kept unchanged in both environments. Pairs valued by the current pre-update models are stored for later iterations. The current weights depend on earlier branch outcomes.

All three models are separate LoRA adapters on one frozen base model and share no parameters beyond it. Only the policy is used at evaluation.

4 Experimental Evaluation

We test whether learning to value predicted consequences raises policy-only success for a comparable amount of real interaction. All methods share a 12-iteration PPO warm-up checkpoint and task order, and are evaluated as policies alone at fixed iterations. WM-PPO and PPO-160 use approximately the same number of real steps. WM-PPO, its policy-channel-only variant, PPO-160, PPO-256, Q-PPO and Wide-Tree-PPO have three training runs each, as does self-teacher OCSD on ALFWorld. WM-PPO’s hyperparameters are set once on ALFWorld; baselines are re-tuned by rules fixed in advance when their settings fail (Section 4.1).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Environments.

ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) is the simpler environment. Its six household task types mostly follow the same routine: find an object, heat, cool or clean it when required, and place it at the requested location. The environment lists admissible actions at every step, leaving search for hidden objects as the main difficulty. We train on 3,553 games and pool evaluation over 140 seen-room and 134 unseen-room games. ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) poses harder elementary science tasks. The 18 task types, fixed before training, all have oracle solutions within 40 steps. Eleven are procedural: the agent must first create or find an intermediate state, such as a mixture, a heated substance, a connected circuit or an organism in another room. The other seven require choosing the right object among candidates. The agent must identify the relevant conditions in long room descriptions and express its actions as free text using 25 templates. Unparseable commands consume a step, and focusing on the wrong object ends the task in failure. These dependencies make the value of a state transition less apparent from the next observation alone: the agent must judge whether a change establishes a condition needed for later success. Appendix B describes ScienceWorld’s fixed training and evaluation sets. In both environments, the reward is 1 for completion within 40 actions and 0 otherwise, with no intermediate rewards. ScienceWorld’s reported progress is part of the observation and is also predicted by the world model.

Model and common start.

All methods train LoRA adapters (rank 64) on a frozen Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025) in non-thinking mode, with responses of at most 256 tokens. The shared PPO warm-up reaches 27.0% success on ALFWorld and 20.8% on ScienceWorld. Its real transitions also train the initial world model. Training then runs for 24 iterations on ALFWorld (13–36) and 48 on ScienceWorld (13–60).

Comparisons.

Table 1 lists the comparisons in three groups. The first group contains established ways of training the same policy: PPO at the two budgets, GRPO and GiGPO (Shao et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025), and three refinements of PPO for multi-turn agents, CAPO (Wang et al., 2026), SO-PPO (Li et al., 2026) and Turn-ratio PPO, a turn-level form of GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025).

The second group contains structural controls. WM-PPO (policy channel only) removes the critic target of Section 3.3; each other control changes one element of that variant. Wide-Tree-PPO keeps the trees and critic training but removes the auxiliary update. Q-PPO values candidates directly with Qω​(st,y)Q_{\omega}(s_{t},y), learned from real returns. Fixed WM keeps the initial world model throughout training (Appendix D).

The third group adds other auxiliary supervision to PPO-160. PaW (Lu et al., 2026) uses the published auxiliary next-observation loss to train the policy on dynamics, without evaluating predicted consequences for task success. Majority-vote labels use ungated self-training on the most common of four sampled actions (Zuo et al., 2025; Shafayat et al., 2025). Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024) uses a frozen Qwen3-32B teacher (Appendix D.2). OCSD (Yang et al., 2026) uses the policy itself or the 32B model as a teacher with access to the observations that followed the action.

Hyperparameters across environments.

WM-PPO uses its ALFWorld hyperparameters unchanged on ScienceWorld, adapting the prompts and the world model’s context and output lengths (Appendix B). Baselines also start from their ALFWorld settings and follow pre-set re-tuning rules if those settings fail. CAPO, SO-PPO and PaW required re-tuning (Appendix D).

Interaction budgets.

The main comparison approximately matches the number of real steps. A real step is an environment step whose action the policy generated and executed, in chains and branches alike, counted from iteration 13; the shared warm-up and the prefix replays are not counted. Because branch points are drawn uniformly along the chain, the 64 chains and 192 branches of a WM-PPO iteration generate about as many real steps as 64×(1+3×12)=16064\times(1+3\times\tfrac{1}{2})=160 episodes, the budget of PPO-160 (Table 1). In practice, WM-PPO executed 3% fewer real steps than PPO-160 on ALFWorld and 13% more on ScienceWorld, where its 128k steps lie between those of PPO-160 (113k) and PPO-256 (156k). We report gains relative to PPO-160. Restoring a branch point by replaying the chain’s prefix brings the total environment calls to about those of the 64×4=25664\times 4=256 episodes of PPO-256, which we include as a supplementary reference. Within this budget, WM-PPO covers 43% of the ALFWorld training tasks, against 100% for PPO.

Evaluation protocol.

Checkpoints are evaluated with the policy alone. Greedy success is the success rate of one greedy episode per evaluation game; pass@1 is the success probability of a single temperature-1 episode, estimated from three episodes per game (pass@3 in Appendix E). Unless stated otherwise, success refers to greedy success. The main comparison reports iteration 36 on ALFWorld and iteration 60 on ScienceWorld, with the checkpoints and hyperparameters of WM-PPO and PPO fixed before evaluation. On ScienceWorld, SO-PPO and PaW each use the best of three settings in Table 2. All three CAPO settings diverged, so its entry uses the checkpoint with the highest greedy success during training, without a significance test (Appendix D). Each seed is represented by its first training run. Differences are tested per evaluation game with two-sided zz-tests on the mean paired difference, uncorrected for multiple comparisons; Appendix E.3 reports each run.

4.2 Policy-only Task Performance

Higher success at comparable real interaction.

On ALFWorld at iteration 36, WM-PPO succeeds on 87.5% of the evaluation games under greedy decoding and on 87.8% under pass@1 evaluation (Table 2); WM-PPO (policy channel only) reaches 88.4% and 89.4%. PPO-160, whose budget of real steps is matched by design, reaches 63.5% and 71.0%, and every run of either variant is above every PPO-160 run. The supplementary PPO-256, with about 50% more real steps, reaches 83.1% and 84.8%, also significantly lower in the per-game comparison.

On ScienceWorld at iteration 60, using the hyperparameters from ALFWorld, WM-PPO reaches 52.9% greedy and 51.6% pass@1 success, against 39.3% and 42.6% for PPO-160 (p<0.001p<0.001). Every WM-PPO run (50.4–54.9% greedy) is above every PPO-160 run (37.7–40.5%). PPO-256, with 22% more real steps, is 9.2 points lower under greedy decoding and 8.0 points lower for pass@1 (p<0.001p<0.001). GRPO and GiGPO remain well below WM-PPO in both environments. They stay below when drawing 40 tasks of 4 episodes each, which covers 91% of the ScienceWorld variations (GiGPO on ScienceWorld only; Appendix E).

ScienceWorld separates the strongest methods.

On the simpler ALFWorld, CAPO, SO-PPO, Turn-ratio PPO, PaW and the two WM-PPO variants cluster at 85.4–88.4% greedy success, approaching the environment’s ceiling. This leaves limited room for success rates to distinguish the methods. The two WM-PPO variants have the highest greedy success, and adding the value channel gives no further gain at this level (87.5% against 88.4%, not significant). Under pass@1, WM-PPO (policy channel only) is ahead of CAPO by 2.7 points, SO-PPO by 6.3 (p<0.001p<0.001) and Turn-ratio PPO by 4.4 (p=0.002p=0.002), and the full method is 4.7 points ahead of SO-PPO (p=0.01p=0.01).

ScienceWorld, with its greater demands on intermediate conditions, gives a clearer separation. WM-PPO reaches 52.9% greedy success against 46.5% for the best of SO-PPO’s three settings, the strongest baseline: a gain of 6.5 points (p=0.004p=0.004). The lead under pass@1 is 2.2 points. Here, the value channel adds 5.8 greedy and 4.4 pass@1 points to the policy channel alone (p<0.001p<0.001; Section 5.2). The PPO refinements change how executed actions are credited; WM-PPO adds comparisons with unexecuted actions and a critic target built from them.

PaW reaches 85.4% success on ALFWorld, 2.1 points below WM-PPO. On ScienceWorld, the single run with its best of three loss weights reaches 35.6%, broadly at PPO-160’s level and slightly below its 39.3%. WM-PPO is 17.4 points higher (p<0.001p<0.001). WM-PPO uses the predicted observations to evaluate which consequences matter for task success.

Higher success than the tested teacher-based methods.

OPD and OCSD use teachers to supply feedback finer than a final 0/1 reward. Self-teacher OCSD improves PPO-160 to 83.0% greedy and 82.7% pass@1 success on ALFWorld over three runs; WM-PPO remains 4.5 and 5.1 points higher (p=0.003p=0.003 and p<0.001p<0.001). On ScienceWorld, self-teacher OCSD is 5.2 points below PPO-160 under greedy decoding (p=0.02p=0.02), level with it for pass@1, and 18.8 and 7.9 points below WM-PPO. The teacher’s judgment separates valid from invalid actions on ALFWorld’s short observations (AUC 0.80), but is inverted on ScienceWorld’s long descriptions (AUC 0.25 and 0.21; Appendix D.2). With the 32B teacher, OCSD reaches 70.1% pass@1 on ALFWorld and is level with PPO-160 on ScienceWorld. Standard OPD ends below PPO-160 in both environments (Appendix D.2). Ungated majority-vote labels reinforce the policy’s repeated choices without information about consequences; success falls to 17.2% on ALFWorld and 25.0% on ScienceWorld. WM-PPO outperforms these methods using a world model and critic trained on the agent’s own interaction.

Performance across runs.

The runs of WM-PPO vary little (86.5–88.3% success on ALFWorld, 50.4–54.9% on ScienceWorld), whereas several baselines vary much more, for example PPO-160 over 52.2–70.1% on ALFWorld and PPO-256 over 33.8–49.3% on ScienceWorld (Appendix E.3).

4.3 Interaction Efficiency

No other method achieves higher success with fewer real steps.

Figure 4 compares each method’s success and real interaction. On ALFWorld, 18 of the 23 other methods lie in the region below and to the right of the evaluated checkpoints of the two WM-PPO variants; on ScienceWorld, 18 of 20 lie below and to the right of WM-PPO’s checkpoints. The methods outside the region used fewer real steps but reached lower success: on ALFWorld, CAPO (with two clipping ranges), Turn-ratio PPO, OCSD and PaW; on ScienceWorld, the tuned SO-PPO and OCSD with the 32B teacher. PPO-256 uses 150k real steps against WM-PPO’s 102k on ALFWorld and 156k against 128k on ScienceWorld, and it ends below WM-PPO in both environments.

The same success takes fewer real steps than with PPO.

Figure 14 in Appendix E plots success against real interaction; Table 14 reports each run’s first evaluated checkpoint above a reference success. By iteration 36 on ALFWorld, the three WM-PPO runs have passed 80% success after 69k–97k real steps and the three runs with the policy channel only after 67k–84k, against 129k–141k for PPO-256. No PPO-160 run has reached 80% by this iteration. The PPO refinements rise fastest early: CAPO and Turn-ratio PPO pass 80% after 63k and 64k real steps. WM-PPO reaches their level by iterations 30–36, and the two variants end with the highest success at iteration 36. On ScienceWorld, WM-PPO separates from PPO-160 after about 30k real steps, and the gap widens to about 6 points by 100k. Its runs pass 45% after 94k–120k real steps and the tuned SO-PPO after 97k, whereas no PPO-160 run passes 45% within its 108k–118k steps. The gap grows over training, in step with the reliability of the comparisons (Section 5.1).

Computation.

Serving and training the world model takes additional GPUs during training. At comparable real steps, an iteration therefore takes 1.3–1.6 times as long as for PPO-160 in wall-clock time and uses 2.7–3.8 times as many GPU-hours (Appendix E.5). This cost stays in training, where the world model and the critic extract the information implicit in environment dynamics; at inference the policy acts alone, without the extra models and GPUs of agents that keep a world model (Chae et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b). The additional computation lets WM-PPO learn more from each real state transition, a tradeoff that is useful when interaction is slow or costly.

5 Understanding the Gains

A transition value estimates the current policy’s chance of success after a candidate action (Equation (6)). This section examines whether these values identify choices that determine task success, how the policy and critic learn from them, and how the trained policy behaves as a result.

5.1 Valuing Predicted State Transitions

Section 2.1 showed that large value gaps identify comparisons the critic orders more reliably. This pattern persists during online training with predicted successors. Late in ScienceWorld training, the preferred action has the better outcome in 84% of branch pairs with different real outcomes in the largest margin bin, while the smaller bins are close to chance (Figure 5a; Table 20).

What a large margin means.

A large margin indicates a large estimated difference in the current policy’s chances of success after the candidate actions. Such a difference can arise when an action commits the agent to a choice that prevents later completion. For example, a ScienceWorld task requires focusing on a non-living thing and moving it into a box. Focusing on air leaves the episode running, but air cannot be moved into the box. Across the three runs, the critics value the predicted successor of focusing on air at 0.03–0.34, compared with 0.54–0.80 for going to the hallway. None of the 24 real continuations after focusing on air succeeds, whereas 19 of 24 succeed after going to the hallway.

Such decisive choices make up a growing part of the largest bin. Its share of pairs with different real outcomes grows from 14% early in training to 33% later, and its realized gain per pair from +0.08 to +0.22 (Table 19), which keeps its gate weight high (Section 5.2).

Predicting successors improves candidate comparisons.

Since a transition value approximates an action value, directly learning a Q network is a natural alternative. The relation from Equation (5),

q^t(a)≈Qπ(st,a)=𝔼[Vπ(st+1)|st,at=a],\hat{q}_{t}(a)\approx Q^{\pi}(s_{t},a)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[V^{\pi}(s_{t+1})\bigm|s_{t},a_{t}=a\bigr],

allows either a direct estimate of QπQ^{\pi} or an estimate through the action’s successor. Q-PPO tests the first route by adding a network Qω​(st,y)Q_{\omega}(s_{t},y) trained on executed actions’ returns. It replaces the world model and critic’s candidate evaluation while retaining the candidates, margins, gate and auxiliary update of WM-PPO (policy channel only). The world model can also learn from the next observation at every executed step, including those in failed episodes. Predicting successors therefore lets the evaluation use supervision about what actions change as well as the returns used to learn value. In ScienceWorld’s largest margin bin, WM-PPO (policy channel only), which differs from Q-PPO only in how candidates are valued, favors the successful action in 85% of training branch pairs with different real outcomes, against 76% for Q-PPO (Table 20). On a shared pool of candidates, the comparisons using the world model are also more accurate at large margins (Figure 5b).

Online updates preserve prediction quality on ScienceWorld.

As the policy learns, it visits new states and proposes different actions, so the world model must keep learning from the resulting transitions. With a fixed world model, prediction accuracy declines as the policy changes (Figure 6a). This decline also affects candidate evaluation: late in training, the Fixed WM run’s largest-margin agreement is 53–64%, against 88–93% for the online run with the same seed (Appendix F.1).

5.2 Learning from Transition Values

The comparisons supply information that additional branches alone do not. Wide-Tree-PPO keeps the trees and critic of WM-PPO (policy channel only) but drops the auxiliary update; across three runs per method, the policy-channel-only variant exceeds it in success by 10.0 percentage points on ALFWorld and 6.3 on ScienceWorld (Table 2). A single offline update on these comparisons alone also improves the policy (Section 2.3).

The value channel adds feedback for the critic. Training the critic toward the mean transition value q¯t\bar{q}_{t} changes how it values the next round’s predicted successors, and hence the preferences used in later policy updates. In ScienceWorld iterations 13–36, the largest-margin comparisons favor the successful action in 78–82% of branch pairs with different outcomes, against 71–74% with the policy channel only (Figure 7b).

A single gate decides when, and how much, these comparisons shape both networks. The same weight wℓ⁡(mt)w_{\ell(m_{t})} scales the policy’s auxiliary advantages and the critic’s auxiliary loss (Equations (8) and (12)); while the gate is closed, the update is ordinary PPO on the trees. Each margin bin earns its weight from the realized gain of its earlier comparisons (Section 3.5).

On ScienceWorld, the gate starts closed and opens as the critic and world model become reliable. The largest bin reaches full weight early in training and keeps it as its comparisons agree more often with real outcomes (Figure 8a; Table 19); its weight still dips when its recent comparisons are less reliable, as around iteration 27. The smaller bins, whose comparisons are close to chance but carry a slightly positive gain, stay at low and fluctuating weights, so their weak signal enters both channels without dominating them.

The value channel feeds this calibration. With more reliable comparisons, the largest bin of WM-PPO opens earlier and stays open; with the policy channel only, the weights are less stable and the largest bin dips in mid-training, so less feedback reaches the two networks (Figure 8a,b). With the fuller feedback, WM-PPO pulls ahead of the policy-channel-only variant from iteration 36 onward (Tables 13 and 13), its critic fits real returns better late in training (explained variance 0.49 against 0.30; Figure 7a), and fewer procedural episodes end in failure on a wrong focus (Figure 7c).

On ALFWorld, the same calibration withdraws feedback as success approaches the ceiling. Few branch pairs then have different outcomes, and equal outcomes contribute no realized gain. The weights fluctuate, and WM-PPO’s largest-margin bin closes at iteration 36 (Figure 8a, lower). With less branch evidence and little room to raise success, the value channel gives no further gain on ALFWorld (Section 4.2).

Fixing the weights shows what this calibration contributes (Figure 9). Full weight rises fastest at first, because it admits the comparisons that the gate still holds back. Later, the near-chance preferences of the smaller bins keep entering at the same weight as the reliable ones, and this copy’s success grows no faster than PPO-160’s; on its own branch records, the gate would have admitted the small bin in only about a quarter of the iterations. Keeping only the largest bin is stable but stays below WM-PPO: it never receives the weak signal that the gate would have drawn from the smaller bins in more than half of its iterations, and it trusts the largest bin from the first iteration, before its comparisons have proven reliable (Appendix F.1). Past the early phase, WM-PPO pulls clearly ahead, and both copies end significantly below it, ordered by the reliability of the margin bins (Section 5.1).

5.3 How the Policy Advances the Task

The trained WM-PPO policy more often completes prerequisites before taking the action that depends on them.

ALFWorld.

WM-PPO more often processes an object before placing it. Its gain over PPO-160 is largest on tasks that require heating, cooling or cleaning before placement: 31.5 points, against 21.5 on plain placing (Figure 10a). The action order helps explain this difference. On processing tasks, WM-PPO places the object before processing it in 17% of episodes in which the object was picked up, against 41% for PPO-160 (Appendix F.5). In the mug-heating game, both policies find the mug; WM-PPO takes it to the microwave, whereas PPO-160 puts it into the cabinet unheated and fails (Figure 11a). PPO-256 also learns the processing order with more interaction; WM-PPO learns it within PPO-160’s budget (Section 4.3).

ScienceWorld.

WM-PPO is more successful on tasks that require intermediate steps and less often commits to an answer before meeting its prerequisites. On the procedural games, it reaches 46.3% success, against 29.6% for PPO-160 (Figure 10c). An accepted focus command commits the agent to an answer, so its timing reveals whether the necessary conditions have been met. On these games, premature focus occurs in 22.0% of WM-PPO’s episodes, against 28.7% for PPO-160 (Figure 10d). The living-thing task illustrates the difference: WM-PPO goes outside and brings a baby beaver to the box, while PPO-160 focuses on a fruit in the starting room and fails (Figure 11b).

6 Related Work

Language agents can draw on information beyond the terminal reward in several ways. Table 3 compares the main approaches by what is predicted, how it is evaluated, where the resulting signal enters training, and what the deployed agent needs.

Observation prediction and dynamics learning.

ECHO, PaW and DGS-WM use real observations as auxiliary prediction targets during RL, so the policy’s own parameters are also trained to predict what its actions produce (Shrivastava et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026). DGS-WM keeps the observation fragments that best support the policy’s real next response, which favors decision-relevant content, but this selection score does not estimate eventual success. Other methods learn the dynamics before task-level policy training. Early Experience offers next-state prediction as a warm-up before imitation, and alternatively mixes self-reflection rationales into imitation (Zhang et al., 2026a); SPA writes true states into the policy’s reasoning before RL (Chen et al., 2026a); and RWML rewards predictions that are close to the true next state (Yu et al., 2026b). In all of these methods, a prediction is judged by how well it matches the real observation. WM-PPO keeps the world model separate and values each predicted change by its effect on task success. The two uses of a world model could be combined.

Predicted outcomes at decision time.

WMA already pairs candidate actions with predicted consequences and a value judgment. With the policy frozen, a world model predicts the next observation of each candidate, a value model scores it, and the best candidate is executed at test time (Chae et al., 2025). WMA also reports that scoring the predicted next state works better than scoring the action alone; Q-PPO makes the corresponding comparison inside training (Section 5.1). WebDreamer plans in the same way with an LLM simulator and a prompted judge (Gu et al., 2025), and QWM selects robot actions by world-model search with a learned Q-function (Dong et al., 2026). ITP lets the agent reflect on imagined multi-step rollouts before acting, either without training or after an expert warm-up and actor-critic RL that learns the imagination length together with the action; in both variants the world model stays in the deployed agent (Liu et al., 2026a).

CoMAP, which is also evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, shares several design choices with WM-PPO (Liu et al., 2026b). Its world model is a separately parameterized copy of the same backbone, retrained on the agent’s own transitions; its labels come from real two-branch rollouts; and a gate decides when to refine. The policy drafts an action, reads the predicted next state and revises the draft after reflection. Training is supervised by expert or corrected actions, and the world model also learns from an EMA teacher that sees the real next state. The prediction thus enters the decision itself, and the world model remains part of the deployed agent. WM-PPO instead turns predicted consequences into training signals through PPO’s critic, and only the policy acts at deployment.

Learned foresight.

Internalizing the Future combines future simulation and success estimation within a single policy (Zhang et al., 2026b). Its mid-training and supervised fine-tuning use foresight traces that DeepSeek V3.1 writes from recorded trajectories, including their future continuations. During RL, the policy generates an imagined plan and a confidence score before reasoning about the next action. A calibration reward trains this score against the terminal outcome, and the scores of corresponding steps, normalized within the group, form an auxiliary step-level advantage in GRPO. The feedback therefore concerns the generated plan rather than a comparison of alternative actions from a shared state. WM-PPO makes that comparison explicitly: the world model predicts the consequences of sampled actions, and PPO’s critic evaluates the resulting states. Both learn from the agent’s own interactions, and their estimates provide feedback for policy and critic updates. At inference, the policy acts without an explicit foresight stage.

Teacher and hindsight feedback.

Distillation supplies token-level feedback from a stronger or better-informed model. In standard on-policy distillation, the student generates its own sequences and a teacher supervises its token distribution on these prefixes (Agarwal et al., 2024). OCSD, in its main configuration, uses the agent’s own earlier policy instead: it scores already generated tokens in matched replay contexts with and without the real later observations, and the score difference rescales the token update while keeping the sign of the original advantage (Yang et al., 2026). Its hindsight also comes from the agent’s own interaction; the difference is that OCSD re-scores executed responses, whereas WM-PPO predicts the consequences of candidates that were not executed. VASPO gives a return-trained critic and a self-teacher access to reference solutions during training and weights tokens by their judgments, on mathematical and logical reasoning (Wu et al., 2026). Like WM-PPO, it deploys the policy alone, but it predicts no state transitions. Section 4.2 compares WM-PPO with OPD and OCSD.

Model-based reinforcement learning.

WM-PPO learns dynamics from the agent’s own interactions and values predicted consequences to guide policy and critic learning. Dyna adds simulated transitions to learning (Sutton, 1991); World Models and Dreamer learn behavior inside a latent model (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2025); MBPO branches short model rollouts from real states (Janner et al., 2019); MVE and STEVE build the critic’s targets from model rollouts (Feinberg et al., 2018; Buckman et al., 2018); and DreamGym replaces the environment of text agents with an LLM simulator (Chen et al., 2026b). Value Prediction Networks and MuZero learn models through values (Oh et al., 2017; Schrittwieser et al., 2020), and value equivalence judges a model by the values it induces (Grimm et al., 2020). In WM-PPO, real rollouts provide every trajectory, the returns that are the critic’s main supervision, and PPO’s advantages. The world model predicts one step for the policy’s candidates, and the critic’s values of these predictions enter learning as candidate comparisons and an auxiliary critic target. This target, the mean transition value, is related to value expansion (Feinberg et al., 2018; Buckman et al., 2018) and supplements regression on real returns. The gate checks the comparisons on real outcomes, in the spirit of value equivalence; the world model itself is trained by likelihood.

Policy improvement over sampled actions.

Valuing actions that were not executed, through a learned critic, is the idea of all-action policy gradients (Allen et al., 2017; Ciosek & Whiteson, 2020). MPO reweights actions sampled from the policy by their estimated values, and AWR reweights the actions in its replay buffer by their estimated advantages (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2019); Muesli regularizes policy-gradient learning toward sampled actions valued with a learned model (Hessel et al., 2021); Sampled and Gumbel MuZero improve the policy over a sampled subset of actions with search (Hubert et al., 2021; Danihelka et al., 2022); and the MC-GRPO variant of ProAct executes candidates sampled at one state in the simulator and values each by its immediate reward plus Monte-Carlo continuations from a random policy (Yu et al., 2026c). The auxiliary term of WM-PPO belongs to this family: it moves probability toward the best of the policy’s own KK samples. Its choices concern how to value these samples and how much to trust their comparisons. WM-PPO values candidates through their predicted successor states and PPO’s critic, then uses outcomes from real branches to calibrate the reliability weights. Expert Iteration, AlphaZero, Dyna-Mind and the first stage of ProAct instead train the policy toward the output of a search (Anthony et al., 2017; Silver et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026c), whereas WM-PPO supplies scalar advantages for the policy’s own samples rather than a target distribution.

ProAct’s MC-PPO variant estimates state values through random-policy rollouts in the simulator, with 1,000 rollouts per state in our Sokoban comparison (Yu et al., 2026c). With comparable numbers of real environment steps, WM-PPO reaches 87.0% success versus 77.3% for MC-PPO, a significant gain of 9.7 percentage points (Appendix E.6).

Value and credit signals for language agents.

QLASS guides action selection with a Q-network trained on exploration trees (Lin et al., 2025); SWEET-RL turns a privileged turn-level critic’s ranking of sampled actions into preference pairs (Zhou et al., 2025); SPA-RL redistributes the final reward into per-step progress rewards (Wang et al., 2025); and process reward models score steps from step-level labels (Lightman et al., 2024). Agent Q trains on sibling pairs whose value gap exceeds a fixed threshold (Putta et al., 2024), whereas the gate of WM-PPO measures which margins are reliable. VinePPO finds that PPO’s value network ranks candidate next steps near chance and replaces it by Monte-Carlo estimates (Kazemnejad et al., 2025), consistent with the small-margin comparisons of Sections 2.1 and 5.1. Group-based methods compare episodes (Shao et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2026) or actions taken at the same state or history (Feng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026); PPO refinements change how advantages and ratios apply within a turn (Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025); and majority-vote self-training rewards agreement with the policy’s most frequent answer (Zuo et al., 2025; Shafayat et al., 2025). WM-PPO complements these forms of credit assignment with learned comparisons of unexecuted alternatives.

7 Discussion and Limitations

The value of a predicted consequence depends on what the current policy can still accomplish from the resulting state. As the policy improves, the same successor can acquire a different value. The world model learns which changes an action produces, and the critic relates those changes to task success using supervision from real returns. Evaluating alternatives in this way lets the policy learn preferences that a few realized outcomes leave unresolved, including between candidates whose observed continuations end with the same reward (Appendix B.2).

Large margins increasingly identify choices that change what remains achievable (Section 5.1). A premature commitment can close off success, while a step that establishes a prerequisite can make it attainable. These are the decisions on which the comparisons are most reliable. The behavioral analyses show the corresponding change in the policy: it more often completes prerequisites before placing an object or committing to an answer. Gains are largest on procedural ScienceWorld tasks and ALFWorld tasks that require heating, cooling or cleaning before placement. They are smaller on forced-choice tasks, where correctness becomes apparent only at the end.

What the world model predicts determines which part of a comparison the critic must supply. Predicted endings supply outcomes directly, and comparisons between continuing successors rely on the critic. For the latter comparisons on ScienceWorld, the value channel raises agreement with real outcomes from 55% to 62% (Appendix F.1). On ALFWorld, no predicted ending settles a comparison, so every comparison rests on the critic. The gate assigns only partial weights there (Figure 8). The value channel improves early candidate comparisons and the critic’s fit to real returns later in training (Figure 7; Section 5.2).

WM-PPO trades additional prediction and evaluation during training for more learning from each real interaction. The benefit is higher success at comparable interaction budgets and fewer steps to reach PPO’s success levels. The extra computation is confined to training; the deployed policy acts alone.

Limitations.

Our main evaluation covers one 4B base model and two text environments, with episodes limited to 40 steps. Branching and gate calibration require a reproducible prefix, as in our deterministic environments, or a saved state. A branch’s first action is sampled conditional on differing from the chain’s action. The update does not correct for this conditioning.

A single greedy prediction of the next observation does not represent uncertainty over possible outcomes. Longer-range effects enter only through the critic. Prediction errors can bias the auxiliary policy advantages and critic targets. Comparisons cover only the policy’s candidates, and many small-margin comparisons receive little or no weight. Extending the benefit to these decision points remains an open problem.

8 Conclusion

WM-PPO uses learned dynamics to evaluate candidate actions through their predicted consequences. A world model trained on real transitions predicts each candidate’s next observation, and PPO’s critic, trained on real returns, values the predicted successor according to the current policy’s chance of success. In the policy channel, comparisons between transition values become auxiliary advantages for the policy’s own samples. In the value channel, the mean transition value becomes a one-step target for the critic at the current state. Real branch outcomes calibrate the weights of both channels. On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the resulting policy achieves higher success than PPO with comparable real interaction. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. Unlike distillation, WM-PPO needs neither a teacher model nor privileged information, yet it also surpasses the teacher-based methods we tested. When deployed alone, the policy more often completes prerequisite steps before committing to an answer or placing an object.
