Appendix A Prompts

The policy and world model use chat prompts, each consisting of a system message followed by one user message. Fields in braces are filled at every step. The policy sees the five most recent observation–action pairs; the action is the last <action> tag of its response (ALFWorld: one of the admissible actions; ScienceWorld: a free-text command, judged by the simulator).

⬇
|System:| You are an expert agent operating in the ALFRED embodied household environment.
|User:|
Your task is to: {task}
Prior to this step, you have already taken {t} step(s). Below are the most recent {k} observations and the corresponding actions you took: [Observation {i}: ’{o_i}’, Action {i}: ’{a_i}’] ...
You are now at step {t+1} and your current observation is: {obs}
Your admissible actions of the current situation are: [{admissible actions}].
Now it’s your turn to take an action. First reason briefly (at most two sentences) about the current situation inside <think> </think> tags. Then choose one admissible action for the current step and present it inside <action> </action> tags.

At the first step the history line is omitted and the observation is the initial room description.

⬇
|System:| You are an expert agent operating in the ScienceWorld environment, a text-based simulator of elementary science experiments.
|User:|
Your task is to: {task}
Rules: ’focus on OBJ’ declares which object the task is about and cannot be undone; focusing on a wrong object ends the task as a failure, so explore first and focus only on the object the task asks about. OBJ must be an object you can refer to now (listed below); LOC is a room name (teleport moves you there directly). Answering questions such as ’which one ...’ is done by focusing on the answer object.
Prior to this step, you have already taken {t} step(s). Below are the most recent {k} observations and the corresponding actions you took:
[Observation {i}: ’{o_i}’, Action {i}: ’{a_i}’] ...
You are now at step {t+1} and your current observation is:
{obs}
Action templates: [look around, look at OBJ, look in OBJ, inventory, task, teleport to LOC, go to LOC, open OBJ, close OBJ, activate OBJ, deactivate OBJ, pick up OBJ, put down OBJ, move OBJ to OBJ, pour OBJ in OBJ, dunk OBJ in OBJ, mix OBJ, use OBJ on OBJ, connect OBJ to OBJ, disconnect OBJ, eat OBJ, flush OBJ, read OBJ, focus on OBJ, wait, wait1].
Objects you can refer to: [{objects}].
Now it’s your turn to take an action. First reason step by step (at most two sentences) inside <think> </think>, then give exactly one action inside <action> </action>.
⬇
|System:| You are a world model of the ALFRED text household environment.
|User:|
Task: {task}
Initial observation: {room}
History of steps so far: [Step {i}: observation ’{o_i}’, action ’{a_i}’] ...
Current observation: {obs}
Admissible actions: [{admissible actions}]
Action taken now: {action}
Predict the environment’s next observation exactly as the environment would print it, inside <obs> </obs>.
⬇
|System:| You are a world model of the ScienceWorld text environment.
|User:|
Task: {task}
Recent actions: [Step {i}: action ’{a_i}’] ... (the last 8 actions)
Current observation:
{obs}
Objects the agent can refer to: [{objects}]
Action taken now: {action}
Predict the environment’s next observation exactly as the environment would print it (action feedback, [Current room], [Inventory] and [score] lines), inside <obs> </obs>.

The world model’s target is the true next observation inside <obs> tags. In ScienceWorld, our environment interface appends [task completed] or [task failed] at an episode ending, which the world model can then predict. The critic receives the predicted successor in the policy’s prompt format, with the prediction as its current observation.

Appendix B Implementation and method details

B.1 One training iteration

Algorithm 2 follows one iteration from real interaction through candidate evaluation to the updates of all three models.

Order within an iteration.

All data collection and candidate evaluation in an iteration use the models from the preceding iteration. The world-model update on the iteration’s executed transitions runs in parallel with the policy and critic updates and replaces the served model when it finishes. Within the trainer, the critic first values every real node and every predicted successor, without gradients. The gate weights, auxiliary rows and auxiliary critic targets q¯t\bar{q}_{t} are then computed, the policy is updated on ordinary and auxiliary rows, and the critic is updated last. The branch pairs of an iteration are valued by the same pre-update critic, binned with that iteration’s thresholds, and used from the next iteration on.

B.2 Advantage estimation on the trees

The critic’s regression.

Besides the regression of Equation (13), the implementation adds a sibling-centered term at the nodes ss with two or more executed children s(c)s^{(c)}, c=1,…,Csc=1,\dots,C_{s}:

∑c=1Cs((Vψ​(s(c))−V¯​(s))−(G⁡(s(c))−G¯​(s)))2,\sum_{c=1}^{C_{s}}\Bigl(\bigl(V_{\psi}(s^{(c)})-\overline{V}(s)\bigr)-\bigl(G(s^{(c)})-\overline{G}(s)\bigr)\Bigr)^{2},

where V¯​(s)\overline{V}(s) and G¯​(s)\overline{G}(s) average over the children of ss, and a child that ends the episode enters with its final reward in place of a value. The term, with weight 1, asks that the centered values of the children match their centered returns, which is the within-state comparison that Equation (7) relies on. Wide-Tree-PPO and Q-PPO use the same term.

The tree estimator.

The raw estimates AGAEA^{\mathrm{GAE}} follow Equation (14) on the tree of a task’s episodes, whose edges are executed (state, response) pairs; the ordinary PPO rows use their whitened values A^t\hat{A}_{t}. RR is the episode’s final reward, 0 also for an episode cut at the 40-step limit, without bootstrapping. If st+1s_{t+1} has a single outgoing edge, A¯GAE​(st+1)=At+1GAE\overline{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}}(s_{t+1})=A^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t+1} and Equation (14) is the usual GAE recursion AtGAE=δt+λ​At+1GAEA^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t}=\delta_{t}+\lambda A^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t+1} with δt=Vψ​(st+1)−Vψ​(st)\delta_{t}=V_{\psi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\psi}(s_{t}).

Two executed actions at the same state.

For two executed actions with non-terminal successors st+1s_{t+1} and st+1′s^{\prime}_{t+1}, Equation (14) gives the difference between their raw advantages,

[Vψ​(st+1)−Vψ​(st+1′)]+λ⁡[A¯GAE​(st+1)−A¯GAE​(st+1′)].\bigl[V_{\psi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\psi}(s^{\prime}_{t+1})\bigr]+\lambda\bigl[\overline{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}}(s_{t+1})-\overline{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}}(s^{\prime}_{t+1})\bigr]. (18)

The first term compares the successor values, and the second carries feedback from their continuations.

A terminated path.

Let the actions at st,…,st+L−1s_{t},\dots,s_{t+L-1} lead to termination after the last of them, with reward RR at that step and zero before, and write Vj=Vψ​(st+j)V_{j}=V_{\psi}(s_{t+j}). Then

AtGAE\displaystyle A^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t} =(V1−V0)+λ⁡(V2−V1)+⋯+λL−2​(VL−1−VL−2)+λL−1​(R−VL−1)\displaystyle=(V_{1}-V_{0})+\lambda(V_{2}-V_{1})+\dots+\lambda^{L-2}(V_{L-1}-V_{L-2})+\lambda^{L-1}(R-V_{L-1}) (19)
=−V0+(1−λ)​∑j=1L−1λj−1​Vj+λL−1​R.\displaystyle=-V_{0}+(1-\lambda)\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}\lambda^{j-1}V_{j}+\lambda^{L-1}R.

The executed continuation, summarized by a λ\lambda-weighted average of the critic’s values along it and the final reward, is compared with the value of the state in which the action was taken. For L=1L=1 the sum is empty and AtGAE=R−V0A^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t}=R-V_{0}; for λ=1\lambda=1 the intermediate values cancel and AtGAE=R−V0A^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t}=R-V_{0}, the Monte-Carlo return minus the baseline. The coefficients of the intermediate values sum to 1−λL−11-\lambda^{L-1}, so with λ=0.95\lambda=0.95 and L=36L=36 the final reward has weight 0.17 and the values along the path 0.83 together, although each single value has a small weight. This follows directly from the definition of GAE (Schulman et al., 2016).

GAE and candidate comparisons.

With the true policy value function and an on-policy continuation, the conditional expectation of AtGAEA^{\mathrm{GAE}}_{t} is the executed action’s true advantage. How informative a sampled estimate is depends on the variances and covariances of the critic’s errors and of the outcome, rather than on the coefficients alone. PPO already provides step-level feedback through its critic and GAE, using state values and returns along the executed paths. The single-path expression in Equation (19) compares the executed continuation with V0=Vψ​(st)V_{0}=V_{\psi}(s_{t}). WM-PPO retains these advantages and extends evaluation to other candidates at the same state through their predicted successors. Their transition values supply direct preferences for the auxiliary policy update. In the policy-channel-only variant, these preferences are the additional policy feedback; critic training and ordinary PPO advantages remain standard.

Equal terminal returns.

In Wide-Tree-PPO on ScienceWorld, all executed candidates have the same terminal return at 82% of its branching states. Those observed outcomes provide no preference among the candidates, although their immediate consequences can differ in whether they advance the task. Appendix G gives a training example in which both continuations succeed but the transition values favor completing the task’s prerequisite first. WM-PPO (policy channel only) outperforms this branch-only control in both environments (Section 5.2).

Value and advantage scales.

On candidate pairs whose estimated true values differ by at least 0.4, the critics’ value differences average 0.02–0.10 in absolute value (Appendix F.4), and the raw advantages of PPO-160 have a median standard deviation of 0.22–0.23 per iteration on ScienceWorld and 0.27–0.30 on ALFWorld before whitening. These numbers indicate the scales involved; they are sampled and normalized differently.

B.3 Settings and components

Table 5 lists the hyperparameters. Table 4 identifies each component’s data, what it learns or computes, and how its output is used.

Task sets.

ScienceWorld training draws up to 120 official training variations per task type (1,228 of 2,106) in a fixed shuffled order with equal weight per task type. The evaluation set is fixed. Within each of the development and test splits, it contains all variations of the seven task types that have few variations and nine evenly spaced variations of every other type: 140 of the 1,053 development and 144 of the 1,060 test variations. Three settings of WM-PPO are environment-specific (Table 5): the prompts, the world model’s context and output length, and the rule for predicted endings, which applies only where observations report the end of an episode. Among the baselines’ settings, only those of CAPO, SO-PPO and PaW differ between the environments, because their ALFWorld settings diverged or lost the action format on ScienceWorld (Appendix D).

Appendix C Diagnostic experiments

The diagnostics in Section 2 test whether the critic can compare actions by valuing their real successors, whether predictions preserve these comparisons, and whether the policy can learn from them. All use the policy and critic of the PPO run continued from the common warm-up to iteration 24 on ALFWorld (Section 2), the 274 evaluation games and per-game paired tests.

Selection with true next states.

At every step, the policy samples four candidates at temperature 1. Each distinct candidate is executed for one step in a copy of the game. The critic values the history extended by the resulting observation and admissible-action list, and the candidate with the highest value is executed in the real game. In the peek control, a candidate that completes the task is taken if one exists; otherwise the majority vote decides.

Pairwise test.

In each evaluation game, one state of the policy’s own episode is drawn at random; the draw is repeated with three random seeds. Every distinct candidate is executed and followed by three independent continuations of the same policy, and the fraction of successes estimates its value. For the 195 candidate pairs with different estimates, this order is compared with the order of the critic’s values of their true next states.

World model for the diagnostic.

The policy played 1,000 training games at temperature 1, executing the first of four samples; every distinct candidate was also executed for one step in a copy of the game, which gives 48k transitions, 44% of them for unexecuted candidates. The world model is a LoRA adapter on the base model, trained for one epoch with the next-observation loss. Accuracy is measured on 1,500 random transitions of the evaluation games, by category of the true next observation: observations determined by information already seen (71% of the transitions; 99.7% predicted exactly), observations revealing objects not seen before (20%; 26% predicted exactly, object F1 0.41), and “Nothing happens” (9%). Choosing with the true observation from which newly revealed objects are removed gives 59.1%, so hidden content affects selection. Where it matters, the world model still provides a prior: it estimates whether the target object is present with an AUC of 0.81 (untrained model: 0.62).

Offline update.

The policy played 500 training games that are not in the world model’s data. At the 8,042 decision points with at least two distinct candidates, the label is the candidate whose predicted successor the critic values highest. One epoch of PPO-clip (lr 10−510^{-5}, about 32k samples) uses the advantages of Equation (4) and no task reward. The KL divergence of the updated policy from the original is 0.017 with world-model labels and 0.033 with majority-vote labels. The evaluation samples at temperature 1, twice per game, without the world model.

Inference-time lookahead on trained policies.

Table 6 applies the selection test of Section 2.1 to trained ALFWorld policies on the 274 evaluation games. At every step, the policy samples four responses at temperature 1. pass@1 executes the first, which is the standard evaluation (three runs). Majority of 4 executes the most frequent action. True next state executes each distinct candidate for one step in a copy of the game, values each extended history with the policy’s own critic of the same iteration, and executes the candidate with the highest value. Predicted next state does the same with the next observation predicted greedily by the world model of the diagnostic in Section 2.2, which is not updated during RL. Each lookahead rule has two runs, and differences are paired per game against pass@1.

Appendix D Baselines

D.1 Budgets, methods and tuning

Budgets.

PPO-160: 160 tasks ×\times 1 episode per iteration; PPO-256: 256 tasks ×\times 1; Wide-Tree-PPO, Q-PPO and Fixed WM: WM-PPO’s trees (64 tasks ×\times (1 chain + 3 branches)); group methods: 20 tasks ×\times 8 episodes, also 40 tasks ×\times 4 for GRPO and, on ScienceWorld, GiGPO (Tree-GRPO: WM-PPO’s trees or 32 trees of 8 leaves, Table 7); PPO refinements and the auxiliary-feedback methods: PPO-160’s sampling. All start from the warm-up checkpoint with the same task order.

Methods.

Wide-Tree-PPO: WM-PPO (policy channel only) without the auxiliary term, that is, the same trees, tree GAE, critic targets and sibling term, and the same ordinary PPO rows of the executed steps. Q-PPO: a third LoRA adapter with a linear head reads the history followed by a candidate response and is regressed on the return below each executed step, plus the sibling term; it is initialized from the warm-up critic and replaces q^\hat{q} in Equation (6); candidates, margins, gate and auxiliary rows are unchanged. Fixed WM: WM-PPO (policy channel only) with a world model that is never updated after its initialization; the policy and the critic are trained, and the gate and the auxiliary rows computed, as in that variant. In both environments it starts from the same initial world model as WM-PPO, trained on the warm-up’s executed transitions (on ScienceWorld, predictions at iteration 13 are token-identical for 78 of 81 shared state–candidate pairs). CAPO (Wang et al., 2026): action-level critic and importance ratio. SO-PPO (Li et al., 2026): one geometric-mean importance ratio per turn with clipping-triggered normalization. Turn-ratio PPO: the GSPO-style turn-level ratio (Zheng et al., 2025) with a narrow clip, as implemented in the CAPO code base (Wang et al., 2026). VAPO-lite (Yue et al., 2025): PPO-160 plus a language-model loss (weight 0.1) on responses of successful episodes. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) and HGPO (He et al., 2026): step-level grouping by identical environment states and by history, ported from their released code. Tree-GRPO (Ji et al., 2026): tree-based group advantages on WM-PPO’s trees. Majority-vote labels: PPO-160 plus four samples per step and auxiliary rows as in Equation (8) with the unique plurality action as the preferred one, weight 1, no gate; computed on PPO-160’s episodes, their total auxiliary weight is about two to three times that of WM-PPO. Standard OPD (Agarwal et al., 2024): a frozen Qwen3-32B in non-thinking mode, which shares the student’s vocabulary, computes the log-probabilities of the executed response given exactly the student’s prompt; every token’s advantage is the whitened GAE advantage plus clip⁡(log⁡πT−log⁡πold,±5)\operatorname{clip}(\log\pi_{T}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{old}},\pm 5), the reverse-KL reward of on-policy distillation, with coefficient 1. OCSD (Yang et al., 2026): the teacher, the policy of the previous iteration (self) or the same Qwen3-32B, computes the log-probability of the executed response with and without the next one or two observations of the episode, but not the current action; the PPO advantage is multiplied by 1+0.5​sign⁡(A)​tanh⁡(Δ/2)1+0.5\,\operatorname{sign}(A)\tanh(\Delta/2), where Δ\Delta is the difference of the two log-probabilities, on the 20% least likely steps per episode, following the released implementation. All OPD and OCSD variants are built on PPO-160 and use its interaction. PaW (Lu et al., 2026): PPO-160 plus PaW’s auxiliary next-observation loss on the policy with the published settings: the clipped loss with ρ=0.2\rho=0.2 on the tokens of the true next observation, applied to the 75% of transitions with the highest action uncertainty, the reward-adaptive weight following the paper’s formula (with the batch’s mean episode return under PPO), and the paper’s 20 prediction prompts. Unlike the original full fine-tuning at learning rate 10−610^{-6}, it trains PPO-160’s LoRA at 10−510^{-5}.

Published results.

Several of these methods report higher ALFWorld success in their own papers. Those results come from different base models, longer training and other budgets. Here, every method shares one base model, one warm-up checkpoint, one task order and a comparable interaction budget, and is reported at fixed iterations.

Tuning rules fixed in advance.

With the published clipping ranges, CAPO (0.001) clipped about 97% of tokens and Turn-ratio PPO (3×10−43\times 10^{-4}) about 85% on ALFWorld, so both barely learned (Table 7). For each of the two, three larger clipping values were tried for one update on the iteration-13 data. The rule chose the smallest value whose clipped-token fraction was at most 20%, or the largest value if none qualified: 0.3 for CAPO and 0.1 for Turn-ratio PPO. On ScienceWorld every method first used its ALFWorld setting unchanged, and only a setting that diverged or lost the action format was re-tuned (CAPO, SO-PPO and PaW); WM-PPO keeps its ALFWorld hyperparameters unchanged. Table 8 lists the ScienceWorld settings.

SO-PPO on ScienceWorld.

On ScienceWorld, SO-PPO with its published clip of 0.2 had a per-iteration KL of 0.07–0.14 from the first update (PPO-160: 0.01–0.02) and collapsed after iteration 36 (15.8% at iteration 60). The rule fixed beforehand was to take the largest of 0.1, 0.05 and 0.02 whose KL after one update on the iteration-13 data was at most 0.02, or the smallest if none qualified. All three exceeded the threshold slightly (0.054, 0.035 and 0.022), so 0.02 was used. For SO-PPO we also ran the clip of 0.1 chosen by the clipped-token rule of CAPO and Turn-ratio PPO. This run did not diverge (per-update KL at most 0.08), but its success peaked at 22.9% among the evaluated checkpoints (iteration 36) and fell to 4.2% at iteration 60, when 92% of its evaluation episodes ended at the step limit. The main table reports the best of the three settings, clip 0.02. The same SO-PPO with clip 0.2 did not collapse on ALFWorld and is reported with the published value there.

CAPO on ScienceWorld.

CAPO with its ALFWorld clip of 0.3 diverged on ScienceWorld at iteration 14, and with 0.1 at iteration 28 (per-update KL spikes of 0.15–0.33, zero success); the last value of the pre-set grid, 0.03, diverged at iteration 18. No setting of the grid remains, so the main table reports, for CAPO on ScienceWorld, the official evaluation of clip 0.1 at iteration 18, the checkpoint with the highest greedy success in the evaluations during training (21.5%; 20.1% at iteration 15, 16.9% at 21 and 9.5% at 24), without a test against WM-PPO. In the official evaluation it reaches 21.1% greedy and 20.0% pass@1 success, after 12.8k real steps; the neighboring checkpoints reach 19.0% (iteration 15) and 19.4% (iteration 21) greedy, so the choice does not depend on which evaluation is used.

Turn-ratio PPO and PaW on ScienceWorld.

Turn-ratio PPO runs on ScienceWorld with its ALFWorld clip of 0.1. It did not diverge (per-update KL of 0.02–0.06, three to five times that of PPO-160), but its success stayed near 25% from iteration 21 on, below PPO-160; because only diverged settings were re-tuned, it keeps this setting. PaW with its published coefficient of 1.0 kept a per-update KL close to that of PPO-160 on ScienceWorld but gradually stopped writing the action tag: the share of training responses without it rose from 0.8% at iteration 16 to 78% at iteration 20, and 67% of its greedy evaluation episodes at iteration 60 end at the step limit; with the coefficients 0.5 and 0.25, the share stays at about 1%, as for PPO-160. Before any result of the two runs, we fixed the coefficients 0.5 and 0.25 and the rule that the main table reports the best of the three settings by greedy success at iteration 60, which is 0.5. On ALFWorld, PaW uses the published coefficient.

D.2 Teacher-based feedback

How strong is the teacher?

Table 9 evaluates candidate teachers as agents in the student’s prompt and action format on the evaluation games. Under greedy decoding and strict parsing of the <action> tag, Qwen3-32B solves 13.5% of the ALFWorld games and 26.4% of the ScienceWorld games. On ALFWorld it often writes its action in its own tool-call format; counting those as actions raises its success to 48.5%. On ScienceWorld, in non-thinking mode, it tends to act without reasoning and to focus early on a wrong object. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct, a second candidate, performs at the same level. The teacher was fixed before these evaluations, which serve only to report its level; no available model of this family was clearly stronger than the trained student, so we did not add a second external teacher.

What OCSD’s judgment tracks.

For every step that OCSD selected during the first self-teacher run, we averaged tanh⁡(Δ/2)\tanh(\Delta/2) over the response tokens, which is OCSD’s judgment of the step, and compared it with labels taken from the true next observation. On ALFWorld (10,019 steps), this judgment separates valid actions from those answered by Nothing happens with an AUC of 0.80, and the adjustment concentrates on the action tokens. On ScienceWorld (8,055 steps), the same judgment is inverted: its AUC is 0.25 for valid against rejected commands and 0.21 for steps that raised the game’s score against steps that did not, and the strongest negative adjustments fall on the reasoning tokens of steps that made progress, which are followed by observations with much new content. The adjustment is bounded and keeps the sign of the advantage; on ScienceWorld, the resulting policy is level with PPO-160 for pass@1.

Standard OPD in training.

On ALFWorld, the student’s responses changed abruptly at the start. The KL divergence from the previous policy was 1.33 in iteration 13; in iteration 14, only 0.5% of the responses contained a parsable action; and the format recovered in iteration 15. The teacher prefers its own tool-call format and suppressed the student’s action tags. On ScienceWorld, the teacher penalized the student’s reasoning heavily (about 63 nats per response early on), and the median response length fell from 77 tokens to 12 by iteration 16. The student led PPO-160 at iteration 36 and then stayed at 31–34% pass@1; the teacher itself reaches 26.4% as a greedy agent (Table 9).

Appendix E Complete results

This appendix reports results for every method at every evaluated iteration (Appendix E.1), the learning curves and the real steps to reference success levels (Appendix E.2), the individual runs, the ScienceWorld task types and the costs per iteration. Marks are as in Table 2; a number in parentheses after a method is its number of runs.

E.1 Results at every evaluated iteration

Tables 11 and 13 list every method at every evaluated iteration, with the real steps up to that iteration and pass@3. On ALFWorld, the methods trained to iteration 55 approach the ceiling of the benchmark. There, WM-PPO succeeds on 88.7% (greedy) and 90.8% (pass@1) and WM-PPO (policy channel only) on 91.4% and 92.9%; PPO-160 reaches 85.0% and 87.3%, PPO-256, with about 1.5 times the real steps, 90.8% and 91.1%, Wide-Tree-PPO (three runs) 87.3% and 90.6%, Fixed WM 93.4% and 92.2%, and PaW 93.1% and 91.8%. With this much training, the differences on ALFWorld lie in how quickly each method gets there (Figure 14, Table 14) rather than in the final level. GRPO with 40 tasks of 4 episodes per iteration, which sees about twice as many tasks as with 20 tasks of 8 episodes, also stays below WM-PPO in both environments, and so does GiGPO on ScienceWorld. On ScienceWorld at iteration 60, SO-PPO has a slightly higher pass@3 than WM-PPO (60.9% against 59.6%).

E.2 Learning curves and steps to a reference success

Figure 12 names every method of Figure 4. Figure 14 gives the learning curves against real interaction, and Table 14 gives the real steps at which each run first passed reference success levels.

E.3 Individual training runs

Table 16 lists every run of the methods with more than one run.

E.4 ScienceWorld by task type

Table 16 breaks down the iteration-60 results of Table 2 by task type. With 6–18 games per type, differences on single types are noisy, so Section 5.3 uses the procedural and forced-choice totals. Three types are solved by none of these methods, and the chemistry-mix tasks are almost never solved.

E.5 Interaction and computation

Table 17 separates the costs per iteration. WM-PPO executes 3% fewer real steps per iteration than PPO-160 on ALFWorld and 13% more on ScienceWorld, where its branches run longer than the budget assumes. It generates about twice as many policy responses (the four candidates per chain step) and adds 1,500–1,950 world-model generations. An iteration takes 40 minutes on ALFWorld against 32 for PPO-160, and 55 minutes against 34 on ScienceWorld. Because WM-PPO also occupies the world-model servers and trainers, its GPU-hours per iteration are about 2.7 and 3.8 times those of PPO-160; these are upper bounds, since shared servers are counted in full. The value channel adds no generation, only a term of the critic’s loss, and its GPU-hours per iteration are similar to those of the policy-channel-only variant. Branching, which Wide-Tree-PPO shares, adds little (1.5 against 1.7 GPU-hours on ALFWorld, 1.9 against 1.7 on ScienceWorld); most of the difference comes from sampling the candidates and from the world model’s predictions and training.

E.6 Sokoban comparison with ProAct’s MC-PPO

We compare WM-PPO with the MC-PPO configuration that ProAct releases for Sokoban (Yu et al., 2026c). The environment is text Sokoban on a 6×66\times 6 grid with one box and at most 15 steps; solving a level gives a terminal reward of 1 and any other ending 0. Training draws from 18,908 levels, and evaluation uses 300 held-out levels with greedy decoding and three temperature-1 samples per level. All three methods start from a common 12-iteration PPO warm-up (52.0% greedy success) and train through iteration 36 with the budgets and hyperparameters of the main experiments: PPO-160 plays 160 levels per iteration, and WM-PPO plays 64 levels with one chain and three branches, both channels and the gate as in Section 3; its initial world model is trained on the 7,962 executed transitions of the warm-up. MC-PPO uses PPO-160’s budget and level schedule and estimates the value of each visited state from 1,000 uniformly random rollouts of at most 15 steps in a copy of the simulator, with TD(0) advantages, discount 0.95 and a Monte-Carlo value weight of 1. ProAct’s GLAD stage, which fine-tunes on reasoning derived from environment search, is not part of this comparison. Over iterations 13–36, MC-PPO performs about 33 million random rollouts, which are not counted as real steps. ProAct’s own Sokoban experiments use one to five boxes and shaped rewards. Each method has one run.

Appendix F Analyses behind Section 5

The following analyses support Section 5. Real branch outcomes test the reliability of transition values (Section 5.1); measurements of prediction quality, advantages and critic values examine how transition values enter learning (Section 5.2); and task trajectories show how the trained policy acts (Section 5.3).

F.1 Branch pairs and the reliability gate

Protocol.

In each iteration, every branch pair (the chain action and the branch action at the branch point, both played to the end) was valued by the iteration’s pre-update models and assigned to a margin bin with that iteration’s thresholds. A pair therefore never contributes to the weights that were applied to it. Pairs whose two returns differ and whose value difference is non-zero are decisive, and a decisive pair is correct when the preferred action has the higher return. WM-PPO’s transition value includes the ending rule: a predicted completion or failure is assigned 1 or 0, and any other successor is valued by the critic. Q-PPO’s value is Qω​(st,y)Q_{\omega}(s_{t},y). Each method’s pairs come from its own sampling, so the two methods are not evaluated on the same pairs. In ScienceWorld, a pair involves focus if either action starts with focus on; this is a property of the action text, not a label of whether the outcome is decided at that step. Intervals: 2,000 bootstrap resamples of (run, iteration) clusters. Data: three runs of each method, iterations 13–60 on ScienceWorld and 13–36 (both WM-PPO variants: to 55) on ALFWorld. Table 19 gives the agreement and the gain by phase and margin bin, and Table 20 splits the late ScienceWorld pairs. For the single Fixed WM run on ScienceWorld, agreement in the largest bin is 0.67, 0.75, 0.53 and 0.64 in the four phases, against 0.72, 0.79, 0.88 and 0.93 for the run of WM-PPO (policy channel only) with the same seed and the same initial world model.

Gain and agreement.

The gain in Equation (16) averages over all branch pairs in a margin bin. Among untied pairs in bin ℓ\ell, let dℓd_{\ell} be the share whose outcomes differ and cℓc_{\ell} the share of these in which the preferred action has the better outcome. Then

gℓ=Pr⁡(Δ​q^≠0∣ℓ)​dℓ​(2​cℓ−1).g_{\ell}=\Pr\bigl(\Delta\hat{q}\neq 0\mid\ell\bigr)\,d_{\ell}\,\bigl(2c_{\ell}-1\bigr). (20)

When the outcomes differ, a correct preference contributes +1+1 and an incorrect preference contributes −1-1; equal outcomes or tied transition values contribute zero. The gate converts the gain and the number of supporting pairs into a training weight through Equation (17).

Early comparisons with the value channel.

Among ScienceWorld branch pairs with different real outcomes, the largest-margin comparisons favor the successful action in 78–82% of cases with the value channel early in training, against 71–74% with the policy channel only (Figure 7b). Later, the two variants reach similar ranking accuracy.

Table 20 splits the late ScienceWorld pairs by the source of the values and by the kind of action. Where one successor is predicted to end the episode, its transition value is the predicted outcome, 1 or 0, rather than a critic value (Equation (6)). These comparisons agree with the real outcome in 95% of the pairs, with or without the value channel. Where both successors continue, the critic orders them, and the value channel raises agreement from 55% to 62% (from 62% to 67% in the largest-margin bin). The value channel thus strengthens the part of the valuation that rests on the critic. The run with a terminal-only value target, which values every candidate not predicted to end the episode at the critic’s value of the current state, reaches 48.2% greedy success at iteration 60, close to the policy-channel-only run with the same seed (48.6%) and below the WM-PPO run with that seed (54.9%; Tables 13 and 16). Against Q-PPO, the difference lies in comparisons that involve a focus command, which commits the agent to an answer and whose consequence the next observation often reveals; without such a command, the two methods are close. Q-PPO’s gate gives more weight in total, a summed weight of about 263 per iteration against 183 for WM-PPO, yet WM-PPO is the more successful of the two (Section 5.1).

Table 22 summarizes the gate per phase of training, averaged over iterations and over the three runs in each environment. Decision pts: chain steps with at least two distinct candidates. Non-zero, Full: the number of these whose margin bin had a positive weight or a weight of 1. Mean wℓw_{\ell}: the weight applied to each margin bin in the iteration’s update; over ScienceWorld iterations 45–60, the window of Table 20, it is 0.15, 0.37 and 1.00. The 13–24 rows include iterations 13 and 14, which use the start-up rule of Table 5. Agreement: fraction of the iteration’s branch pairs with different outcomes in which the action with the higher value had the better outcome. Pairs: number of such pairs per iteration. Gain: the realized gain of Equation (16) on the iteration’s pairs, per margin bin.

Gate ablation.

Two copies of the first WM-PPO run on ScienceWorld fix the three bin weights from iteration 13 onward; both channels, the world-model updates and all other settings are unchanged. Weights (1,1,1)(1,1,1) admit every comparison at full weight, and weights (0,0,1)(0,0,1) (top bin) keep only the largest-margin bin. Relative to the calibrated first run, the summed gate weight per iteration is 1.9–2.8 times as large without the gate and 0.4–0.7 times as large with the top bin (ranges over the four training phases). Applying the gate rule to each copy’s own branch records shows what calibration would have admitted: in the top-bin copy, positive weight for the small and middle bins in 28 and 27 of 48 iterations; in the full-weight copy, positive weight for the small bin in only 11 of 48 iterations, where that bin’s mean realized gain is −0.005-0.005. Table 21 gives the official evaluations.

Gate coverage with the value channel.

On ScienceWorld, the value channel increases the number of evaluated states with nonzero weight early in training. In iterations 13–24 and 25–36, WM-PPO admits 327 states per iteration in each phase, against 281 and 275 with the policy channel only, averaged over iterations and the three runs. The corresponding full-weight counts are 56 against 41 in the first phase and 98 against 75 in the second. The largest-margin bin of WM-PPO remains at full weight from iteration 29 onward; the policy-channel-only variant’s mean weight falls during iterations 28–39, reaching about 0.67 (Figure 8a,b).

F.2 World-model predictions along training

Table 23 gives the statistics behind Figure 6a,b in four phases of training. At each evaluated chain state, we compare that iteration’s world model’s prediction for the executed action with the observation the environment returned. Exact: the two match after whitespace normalization. Rejections: recall and precision of the prediction that the simulator rejects the command. Endings foreseen: fraction of the steps that ended the episode for which the world model predicted an ending. On ScienceWorld, the online world model (the three policy-channel-only runs) is compared with the run whose world model is fixed, starting from the same initial model; each is measured on the states visited by its own policy. By phase, the online model predicts 84–86% of the executed steps’ observations exactly throughout training, whereas the fixed model falls from 81% to 68%. The online model also foresees 73–75% of the steps that end an episode, against about half for the fixed model. Figure 6 shows the same quantities in windows of three iterations.

F.3 Recomputed advantages

Simulator feedback makes accepted and rejected commands a direct probe of how learning signals distinguish candidates at the same state. A rejected command usually leaves the task recoverable and rarely determines its final outcome. The following measurements compare advantages and candidate preferences; Section F.4 reports the critics’ comparisons during training and at evaluation, and Section F.5 reports the policy’s command choices during training.

To measure how the advantages separate useful from useless steps, we recomputed the raw tree-GAE advantages of ScienceWorld iterations 15, 30, 45 and 60 for the three runs each of PPO-160, WM-PPO, WM-PPO (policy channel only) and Wide-Tree-PPO. The recomputation uses the critic of training (saved at the end of the preceding iteration) and the training code’s estimator (γ=1\gamma=1, λ=0.95\lambda=0.95). The means and standard deviations of the recomputed advantages match the training logs to four decimals in all 48 (run, iteration) cases, and so do the counts of auxiliary rows of both WM-PPO variants. Executed non-terminal edges are classified by the true next observation as rejected (the simulator’s No known action matches that input) or accepted. Table 24 summarizes the results, and Table 25 gives the counts.

The first term of the advantage, Vψ​(st+1)−Vψ​(st)V_{\psi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\psi}(s_{t}), averages −0.003-0.003 for rejected and +0.002+0.002 for accepted commands under PPO-160’s critics (−0.005-0.005 and +0.003+0.003 for Wide-Tree-PPO, −0.005-0.005 and +0.003+0.003 for WM-PPO, −0.006-0.006 and +0.003+0.003 for the policy-only variant). At states where both kinds were executed, the accepted command has the higher advantage in 58% of 476 pairs for Wide-Tree-PPO, in 61% of 431 pairs for WM-PPO and in 56% of 476 pairs for the policy-only variant; in 77%, 84% and 81% of these pairs, the two advantages differ by less than 0.25 standard deviations. The auxiliary comparisons were examined at the states with nonzero weight at which candidates were predicted to be rejected and accepted (prediction precision 0.99): 1,789 states for WM-PPO and 1,560 for the policy-only variant. At these states, the comparison prefers an accepted candidate in 64% for WM-PPO (78% at full weight and 60% at partial weight; mean weight 0.49) and in 67% for the policy-only variant (80% and 64%; mean weight 0.44). In the remaining third, mostly in partially weighted bins, the critic values the predicted successor of the rejected command, which leaves the task where it was, above those of the alternatives. These are comparisons in which the critic values both successors (Table 20).

The same measurement on ALFWorld.

For ALFWorld, we recomputed iterations 15, 24, 30 and 36 of the same methods in the same way, and the logs again match to four decimals. Executed non-terminal steps are classified from the true next observation. Advancing steps take the task object, heat, cool or clean it, place it in the target receptacle, or use the desk lamp. Wasted steps receive Nothing happens or go to a location already visited in the episode before the task object has been taken (returning to the target receptacle is not counted). Under PPO-160’s critics, the first term of the advantage averages +0.014+0.014 for advancing steps and −0.011-0.011 and −0.009-0.009 for the two kinds of wasted step. The comparisons were examined at the states with nonzero weight at which both an advancing and a wasted candidate were sampled (219 for WM-PPO, 116 for the policy-only variant); the preferred candidate is advancing at 59% and 66% of these states and wasted at 26% and 21% (mean weights 0.64 and 0.60). Few states have both kinds of executed step (21–52 pairs per method; Table 24), and these states differ from those of the comparisons. Unlike on ScienceWorld, the advantages already separate the two kinds of step: the gap between their mean advantages is 0.41 standard deviations under PPO-160’s critics, against 0.10 on ScienceWorld (Table 25).

F.4 Candidates at evaluation states

At the decision points of the final (iteration-60) PPO-160 and WM-PPO policies on 60 procedural ScienceWorld evaluation games, every distinct candidate among four samples was executed in a copy of the game, and the same policy then played the episode to the end five times. The success rate estimates the candidate’s true value. With four candidates and five continuations each, no candidate led to a success in any continuation at 73.5% of PPO-160’s decision points and at 55.9% of WM-PPO’s (Figure 15a). At such points, these continuations cannot tell the candidates apart, although the candidates’ true values need not be exactly zero. Figure 16 shows how three critics order the true next states of the candidate pairs whose estimates differ. On both sets of decision points, all three critics are close to chance (47–54% of all such pairs and 48–54% of the 20% with the largest value gap). With five continuations, each estimate has a standard error of up to about 0.2.

Rejected commands in ScienceWorld: detection.

During training, on the executed steps of the evaluated decision points, the online world model of WM-PPO (policy channel only) predicts 98–99% of the rejections with a precision of 0.99 (Table 23). On evaluation states, the recall is lower. On 80 procedural evaluation games, the final WM-PPO and PPO-160 policies played as in training. At every decision point, each distinct candidate among four samples was executed in a copy of the game and also predicted by a final world model. Of 1,717 candidates on WM-PPO’s decision points, 670 were rejected by the simulator; the world model of the first WM-PPO run predicted a rejection for 582 candidates, 580 of them correctly (recall 0.87, precision 1.00). On PPO-160’s decision points, the world model of the first policy-channel-only run finds the rejections among 664 of 1,760 candidates with recall 0.84 and precision 0.99.

Rejected commands: comparisons during training.

Of the 17,385 real branch pairs of iterations 13–60 in the three runs of WM-PPO (policy channel only), 3,835 have exactly one action predicted to be rejected and no predicted ending. The critic of that iteration valued the accepted action higher in 67% of them (59% in the smallest-margin bin, 73% in the middle bin and 74% in the largest). By phase, the rate is 64%, 70%, 69% and 67% (iterations 13–24, 25–36, 37–48 and 49–60), and in the largest bin of iterations 49–60 it is 78%. In the three runs of WM-PPO, 3,971 pairs qualify; the rate is 69% (60%, 72% and 81% by margin bin; 63%, 72%, 74% and 68% by phase), and in the largest bin of iterations 49–60 it is 90% (171 pairs).

Rejected commands: final critics.

On the evaluation states of the true-outcome test (Appendix F.4; Figure 15b), we consider pairs of non-terminal candidates of which the simulator accepted one and rejected the other. On PPO-160’s decision points (481 pairs), the iteration-60 critics value the accepted command’s true next state higher in 65% (PPO-160), 80% (Wide-Tree-PPO) and 60% (WM-PPO) of the pairs; on WM-PPO’s decision points (430 pairs), the rates are 76%, 80% and 60% (53% for the critic of a second WM-PPO run). A second run of the test on the 80 procedural evaluation games described above gives the same ordering (PPO-160 72–76%, Wide-Tree-PPO 80–83%, WM-PPO 58–59%). The critics of PPO-160 and Wide-Tree-PPO separate rejected commands more sharply, while their policies keep issuing them (37.5% and 40.2% of procedural commands late in training, means over runs); the policy of WM-PPO issues fewer (29.5%). The final critic of WM-PPO (policy channel only) orders 43–48% of these pairs correctly (45–47% in the separate test).

F.5 Behavior of the trained policies

Section 5.3 takes success rates from the official evaluation and behavior rates from greedy re-runs of the final checkpoints that log every step. Greedy decoding on the inference server is not bit-exact, and the re-runs reproduce the official per-game outcome for 94–99% of the ALFWorld and 91.5–96.5% of the ScienceWorld games. The pooled behavior differences of Figure 10b do not hold in every run: one PPO-160 run completes the processing in all 91 of its picked-up episodes and places the object before processing it in 10.

Tables 26 and 27 are computed from the training chains (the episode’s own path, without branches), decoded into actions and observations. Table 26 covers procedural ScienceWorld tasks in the first and last windows of training for nine methods, and Table 27 covers ALFWorld in iterations 34–36, pooling the runs of each method. One pattern is not discussed method by method in Section 5.3: the tuned SO-PPO ends slightly fewer ScienceWorld evaluation episodes with a failure than WM-PPO (27.1% against 30.3%) but more at the step limit (26.4% against 16.8%).

Premature focus.

Figure 10d counts, in the greedy re-runs of the 188 procedural ScienceWorld games, the episodes whose first accepted focus on command comes before the state that the answer depends on exists; the definition was fixed per task type before counting. In the chemistry tasks (52 games), the first focus precedes any mix whose feedback reports a product; in the melting-point task (18), the focus on an answer box precedes any thermometer reading; in the find tasks (72), the first focus is on an object that does not qualify, and the simulator ends the episode as failed. The remaining 46 procedural games ask for a focus first or are answered by placing an object, so they cannot contain a premature focus. The re-runs reproduce the official per-game outcome for 89–97% of the games. Over all procedural games, the premature share is 22.0% for WM-PPO, 26.8% for PPO-256, 28.7% for PPO-160 and 28.7% for the policy-channel-only variant (per run 13.3–35.1%, 23.9–30.9%, 25.5–33.0% and 25.5–34.0%); per game, the share of WM-PPO is lower than that of PPO-256 in 37 games and higher in 25. Split by task type after this count, it is 6.9%, 19.0%, 19.4% and 21.3% on the find tasks (per game, WM-PPO is lower than PPO-256 in 14 games and higher in 1), 64.8%, 79.6%, 74.1% and 83.3% on the melting-point task, and 47.4%, 42.9%, 51.3% and 45.5% on the chemistry tasks, where one WM-PPO run focuses prematurely in all of its chemistry episodes. A premature focus ends in failure in the chemistry and find tasks; in the melting-point task, 20 of 35 such WM-PPO episodes still name the right box.

Further cases.

Table 28 lists further evaluation games from the greedy re-runs in which the decisive difference is an intermediate operation or the direction of search. At iteration 31 of a run with the policy channel only, the policy held a dirty pot and sampled go to sinkbasin 1 twice and move pot 1 to stoveburner 2 twice. The world model predicted You arrive at sinkbasin 1… and You move the pot 1 to the stoveburner 2, and the critic valued the two predicted successors at 0.952 and 0.950. The bin of this small margin had weight 0.85 in that iteration, so the four samples received auxiliary advantages of +0.42+0.42, +0.42+0.42, −0.42-0.42 and −0.42-0.42. PPO-160 made the second move in the same game one iteration later and failed. In one further ALFWorld game (heating an apple), the final world model and critic of one run rank the fridge slightly above the microwave (1.051 against 1.044; another run ranks the microwave first), although WM-PPO succeeds in all three runs. We therefore report these additional cases without assigning decisive-state values to them.

Appendix G Inputs and outputs of the models

In the training example of Figure 19, the task requires making orange paint and then focusing on it. The bowl currently contains red and yellow paint, but the orange paint does not yet exist. The world model predicts that ‘mix bowl’ will produce orange paint, whereas ‘focus on orange paint’ will be rejected and leave the bowl unchanged; both predictions match the environment. The critic assigns a higher transition value to the successor in which the paint has been made. Although both real continuations ultimately succeed, these immediate consequences supply a preference for mixing before focusing. Of the four sampled responses, the three ‘mix bowl’ samples each receive +14+\tfrac{1}{4} and the ‘focus on orange paint’ sample receives −34-\tfrac{3}{4}, times the bin’s weight. These auxiliary advantages raise the log-probability of the mixing responses relative to the focus response (Equation (9)).

Table 29 distinguishes the simulator’s internal state, which no model sees; the prompt state sts_{t} read by the policy and critic; and the next observation o^t+1\hat{o}_{t+1} generated by the world model. Two evaluated decision points from the training logs follow verbatim. The world-model input is not logged as text; we rebuilt it from the logged transition record with the training prompt function, which reproduces the logged policy prompt exactly. The prediction and the critic input are decoded from the logged token ids, and re-assembling the critic input from the decoded prediction reproduces those ids. The raw world-model generation and the critic’s individual values of predicted successors are not logged; the trainer logs only the value difference of each branch pair.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
